The satraps and tributary kings under Darius, or Cyaxares.<div eID="gen19222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his dominion--</hi>the king of Media's dominion. <div eID="gen19223" type="x-p"/>
entries.28d652ec39323cf659b964b28da682fe105dfd48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10732"/><div sID="gen19224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10732"/><hi type="bold">29. land shall tremble ... every purpose of ... Lord shall be performed--</hi>elegant antithesis between the trembling of the land or earth, and the stability of "every purpose of the Lord" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.3">Psa 46:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen19224" type="x-p"/>
entries.9007b1ffb35237389659e17d97388ace33da49db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10733"/><div sID="gen19225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10733"/><hi type="bold">30. forborne to fight--</hi>for the city was not taken by force of arms, but by stratagem, according to the counsel given to Cyrus by two eunuchs of Belshazzar who deserted.<div eID="gen19225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remained in ... holds--</hi>not daring to go forth to fight; many, with Nabonidus, withdrew to the fortified city Borsippa. <div eID="gen19226" type="x-p"/>
entries.e43703f46132720f87d9a660e7f8f59ee96443ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10734"/><div sID="gen19227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10734"/>31. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jr 50:24</reference>).<div eID="gen19227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">One post--</hi>One courier after another shall announce the capture of the city. The couriers despatched from the walls, where Cyrus enters, shall "meet" those sent by the king. Their confused running to and fro would result from the sudden panic at the entrance of Cyrus into the city, which he had so long besieged ineffectually; the Babylonians had laughed at his attempts and were feasting at the time without fear.<div eID="gen19228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken at one end--</hi>which was not known for a long time to the king and his courtiers feasting in the middle of the city; so great was its extent that, when the city was already three days in the enemy's hands, the fact was not known in some parts of the city [Aristotle, Politics, 3.2]. <div eID="gen19229" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfaad1cbad929b821751e2eae1a29761485608bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10735"/><div sID="gen19230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10735"/><hi type="bold">32. passages are stopped--</hi>The guarded fords of the Euphrates are occupied by the enemy (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>).<div eID="gen19230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reeds ... burned--</hi>literally, "the marsh." After draining off the river, Cyrus "burned" the stockade of dense tree-like "reeds" on its banks, forming the outworks of the city's fortifications. The burning of these would give the appearance of the marsh or river itself being on "fire." <div eID="gen19231" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2c4b6940dc00d7cf1254c92418f718fe1a861c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10736"/><div sID="gen19232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10736"/><hi type="bold">33. like a threshing-floor, it is time to thresh her--</hi>rather, "like a threshing-floor at the time of threshing," or "at the time when it is trodden." The treading, or threshing, here put before the harvest, out of the natural order, because the prominent thought is the treading down or destruction of Babylon. In the East the treading out of the corn took place only at harvest-time. Babylon is like a threshing-floor not trodden for a long time; but the time of harvest, when her citizens shall be trodden under foot, shall come [Calvin]. "Like a threshing-floor full of corn, so is Babylon now full of riches, but the time of harvest shall come, when all her prosperity shall be cut off" [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Grotius distinguishes the "harvest" from the "threshing"; the former is the slaying of her citizens, the latter the pillaging and destruction of the city (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen19232" type="x-p"/>
entries.10b31a1ac1eed368f19a06f40bca3841c349ba46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10737"/><div sID="gen19233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10737"/><hi type="bold">34. me--</hi>Zion speaks. Her groans are what bring down retribution in kind on Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">Jr 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>, 17, 20).<div eID="gen19233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">empty vessel--</hi>He has drained me out.<div eID="gen19234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dragon--</hi>The serpent often "swallows" its prey whole; or a sea monster [Grotius].<div eID="gen19235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled his belly ... cast me out--</hi>like a beast, which, having "filled" himself to satiety, "casts out" the rest [Calvin]. After filling all his storehouses with my goods, he has cast me out of this land [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19236" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d08928b927c1d205c8220f74afd4c3fff7f9ac4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10738"/><div sID="gen19237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10738"/><hi type="bold">35. my flesh--</hi>which Nebuchadnezzar hath "devoured" (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jr 51:34</reference>). Zion thus calls her kinsmen (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Ro 11:14</reference>) slain throughout the country or carried captives to Babylon [Grotius]. Or, as "my blood" follows, it and "my flesh" constitute the whole man: Zion, in its totality, its citizens and all its substance, have been a prey to Babylon's violence (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>). <div eID="gen19237" type="x-p"/>
entries.06b5e674cc7739591a9aa7c985b5c0b17e32f6a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10739"/><div sID="gen19238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10739"/><hi type="bold">36. plead ... cause--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">Jr 50:34</reference>).<div eID="gen19238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sea--</hi>the Euphrates (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>, "sea," that is, the Nile (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Is 21:1</reference>). <div eID="gen19239" type="x-p"/>
entries.62f34fc9807c75db8c3709d44e6f27072c780942: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10740"/><div sID="gen19240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10740"/>37. (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.26">Jr 50:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19240" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7fca519578d36e22ac9f9ebdeb7cd0c0f71dd2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10741"/><div sID="gen19241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10741"/>38-39. The capture of Babylon was effected on the night of a festival in honor of its idols.<div eID="gen19241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roar ... yell--</hi>The Babylonians were shouting in drunken revelry (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">Da 5:4</reference>). <div eID="gen19242" type="x-p"/>
entries.e131cbb4203f62b38d475c2b627acf9f1425936f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10743"/><div sID="gen19245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10743"/><hi type="bold">41. Sheshach--</hi>Babylon (compare Note, see <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jr 25:26</reference>); called so from the goddess Shach, to whom a five days' festival was kept, during which, as in the Roman Saturnalia, the most unbridled licentiousness was permitted; slaves ruled their masters, and in every house one called Zogan, arrayed in a royal garment, was chosen to rule all the rest. He calls Babylon "Sheshach," to imply that it was during this feast the city was taken [Scaliger]. <div eID="gen19245" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bd8b01e13cb6c2449a2d4d927492c855236af4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10744"/><div sID="gen19246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10744"/><hi type="bold">42. The sea--</hi>the host of Median invaders. The image (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.47.2">Jr 47:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">8</reference>) is appropriately taken from the Euphrates, which, overflowing in spring, is like a "sea" near Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.36">32, 36</reference>). <div eID="gen19246" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0d0d56888cf8a6863dd6a56ca44373097127631: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10745"/><div sID="gen19247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10745"/><hi type="bold">43. Her cities--</hi>the cities, her dependencies. So, "Jerusalem and the cities thereof" (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jr 34:1</reference>). Or, the "cities" are the inner and outer cities, the two parts into which Babylon was divided by the Euphrates [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19247" type="x-p"/>
entries.56fa9521c43daf69e637c490dd3083bc7f88e0f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10746"/><div sID="gen19248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10746"/><hi type="bold">44. Bel ... swallowed--</hi>in allusion to the many sacrifices to the idol which its priests pretended it swallowed at night; or rather, the precious gifts taken from other nations and offered to it (which it is said to have "swallowed"; compare "devoured," "swallowed," <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jr 51:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">Jr 50:17</reference>), which it should have to disgorge (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jr 50:37</reference>). Of these gifts were the vessels of Jehovah's temple in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.7">2Ch 36:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.1.2">Da 1:2</reference>). The restoration of these, as foretold here, is recorded in <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7-Ezra.1.11">Ezr 1:7-11</reference>.<div eID="gen19248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flow--</hi>as a river; fitly depicting the influx of pilgrims of all "nations" to the idol. <div eID="gen19249" type="x-p"/>
entries.5be22879c614f6a08b66ef344f6c26ca7a48ef5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10747"/><div sID="gen19250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10747"/>45-46. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">Jr 51:6</reference>). <div eID="gen19250" type="x-p"/>
entries.8459d186444401f69c52ea6375089f39948b40a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10749"/><div sID="gen19254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10749"/>47. Grotius translates, "Because then (namely, on the third year) the time shall have come that," &c.<div eID="gen19254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confounded--</hi>at seeing their gods powerless to help them.<div eID="gen19255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her slain--</hi>in retribution for "Israel's slain" (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.49">Jr 51:49</reference>) who fell by her hand. Grotius translates, "her dancers," as in <reference osisRef="Judg.21.21">Jud 21:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.21.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference>, the same Hebrew word is translated, alluding to the dancing revelry of the festival during which Cyrus took Babylon. <div eID="gen19256" type="x-p"/>
entries.472b48c2287d4b12da0a8e6781df810fed3f91b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10750"/><div sID="gen19257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10750"/><hi type="bold">48. heaven ... earth ... sing for Babylon--</hi>(Is 14:7-13; 44:23; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">Re 18:20</reference>). <div eID="gen19257" type="x-p"/>
entries.f116ebb6cf14d4460091ca84e289d74849fae469: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10751"/><div sID="gen19258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10751"/><hi type="bold">49. caused ... to fall--</hi>literally, "has been for the falling," that is, as Babylon made this its one aim to fill all places with the slain of Israel, so at Babylon shall all the slain of that whole land (not as English Version, "of all the earth") [Maurer]. Henderson translates, "Babylon also shall fall, ye slain of Israel. Those also of Babylon shall fall, O ye slain of all the earth." But, "in the midst of her," <reference osisRef="Jer.51.47">Jr 51:47</reference>, plainly answers to "at Babylon," <reference osisRef="Jer.51.49">Jr 51:49</reference>, English Version. <div eID="gen19258" type="x-p"/>
entries.98d5e0f4a1db62a2c3acfda3108f3a628660da4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10752"/><div sID="gen19259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10752"/><hi type="bold">50. escaped ... sword--</hi>namely, of the Medes. So great will be the slaughter that even some of God's people shall be involved in it, as they had deserved.<div eID="gen19259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afar off--</hi>though ye are banished far off from where ye used formerly to worship God.<div eID="gen19260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let Jerusalem come into your mind--</hi>While in exile remember your temple and city, so as to prefer them to all the rest of the world wherever ye may be (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>). <div eID="gen19261" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4767f045319a0db8992ffb9bd79679cf6f8ddf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10753"/><div sID="gen19262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10753"/>51. The prophet anticipates the Jews' reply; I know you will say in despair, "We are confounded," &c. "Wherefore (God saith to you) behold, I will," &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.52">Jr 51:52</reference>) [Calvin]. I prefer taking <reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jr 51:51</reference> as the prayer which the Jews are directed to offer in exile (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.50">Jr 51:50</reference>), "let Jerusalem come into your mind" (and say in prayer to God), "We are confounded." This view is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Ps.44.15">Psa 44:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.4">79:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.17-Ps.102.20">102:17-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>.<div eID="gen19262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for strangers--</hi>The "reproach," which especially has stung us, came when they taunted us with the fact that they had burned the temple, our peculiar glory, as though our religion was a thing of naught. <div eID="gen19263" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a2c8ecfa5adf2f035615c26298b2148fde5b902: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10754"/><div sID="gen19264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10754"/><hi type="bold">52. Wherefore--</hi>because of these sighs of the Jews directed to God (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.21">Jr 51:21</reference>).<div eID="gen19264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... judgment upon ... images--</hi>in opposition to the Babylonian taunt that Jehovah's religion was a thing of naught, since they had burned His temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jr 51:51</reference>): I will show that, though I have thus visited the Jews neglect of Me, yet those gods of Babylon cannot save themselves, much less their votaries, who shall "through all her land" lie and "groan" with wounds. <div eID="gen19265" type="x-p"/>
entries.308a4d3f0e7d907c338a7634f94fac1876792d61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10755"/><div sID="gen19266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10755"/>53. We are not to measure God's power by what seems to our perceptions natural or probable. Compare Ob 4 as to Edom (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">Am 9:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19266" type="x-p"/>
entries.f74627addbd761fc5b71bc578d9f86483a7df165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10756"/><div sID="gen19267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10756"/><hi type="bold">55. great voice--</hi>Where once was the great din of a mighty city, there shall be the silence of death [Vatablus]. Or, the "great voice" of the revellers (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.38">Jr 51:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Is 22:2</reference>). Or, the voice of mighty boasting [Calvin], (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.53">Jr 51:53</reference>).<div eID="gen19267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her waves--</hi>"when" her calamities shall cause her to give forth a widely different "voice," even such a one as the waves give that lash the shores (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.42">Jr 51:42</reference>) [Grotius]. Or, "when" is connected thus: "the great voice" in her, when her "waves," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>). Calvin translates, "their waves," that is, the Medes bursting on her as impetuous waves; so <reference osisRef="Jer.51.42">Jr 51:42</reference>. But the parallel, "a great voice," belongs to her, therefore the wave-like "roar" of "their voice" ought also belong to her (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.54">Jr 51:54</reference>). The "great voice" of commercial din, boasting, and feasting, is "destroyed"; but in its stead there is the wave-like roar of her voice in her "destruction" (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.54">Jr 51:54</reference>). <div eID="gen19268" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1cfdb5462848c571bc142e6825fd28e6e363499: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10757"/><div sID="gen19269" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10757"/><hi type="bold">56. taken--</hi>when they were least expecting it, and in such a way that resistance was impossible. <div eID="gen19269" type="x-p"/>
entries.189b743d902305a2abf4485da5a6fc052820c6e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10758"/><div sID="gen19270" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10758"/>57. (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jr 51:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1">Da 5:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen19270" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef226984d5551e2a17bc5e7484252a9537434699: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10759"/><div sID="gen19271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10759"/><hi type="bold">58. broad walls--</hi>eighty-seven feet broad [Rosenmuller]; fifty cubits [Grotius]. A chariot of four horses abreast could meet another on it without collision. The walls were two hundred cubits high, and four hundred and eighty-five stadia, or sixty miles in extent.<div eID="gen19271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gates--</hi>one hundred in number, of brass; twenty-five on each of the four sides, the city being square; between the gates were two hundred and fifty towers. Berosus says triple walls encompassed the outer, and the same number the inner city. Cyrus caused the outer walls to be demolished. Taking the extent of the walls to be three hundred and sixty-five stadia, as Diodorus states, it is said two hundred thousand men completed a stadium each day, so that the whole was completed in one year.<div eID="gen19272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labour ... in the fire--</hi>The event will show that the builders of the walls have "labored" only for the "fire" in which they shall be consumed, "In the fire" answers to the parallel, "burned with fire." Translate, "shall have labored in vain," &c. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job 3:14</reference>, "built desolate places for themselves," that is, grand places, soon about to be desolate ruins. Jeremiah has in view here <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Ha 2:13</reference>. <div eID="gen19273" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7c40def20cc34a80632d0ca4cc69c34ba6aa081: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10760"/><div sID="gen19274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10760"/>59-64. A special copy of the prophecy prepared by Jeremiah was delivered to Seraiah, to console the Jews in their Babylonian exile. Though he was to throw it into the Euphrates, a symbol of Babylon's fate, no doubt he retained the substance in memory, so as to be able orally to communicate it to his countrymen.<div eID="gen19274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went with Zedekiah--</hi>rather, "in behalf of Zedekiah"; sent by Zedekiah to appease Nebuchadnezzar's anger at his revolt [Calvin].<div eID="gen19275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fourth year--</hi>so that Jeremiah's prediction of Babylon's downfall was thus solemnly written and sealed by a symbolical action, six whole years before the capture of Jerusalem by the Babylonians.<div eID="gen19276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quiet prince--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.9">1Ch 22:9</reference>, "a man of rest." Seraiah was not one of the courtiers hostile to God's prophets, but "quiet" and docile; ready to execute Jeremiah's commission, notwithstanding the risk attending it. Glassius translates, "prince of Menuchah" (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.52">1Ch 2:52</reference>, Margin). Maurer translates, "commander of the caravan," on whom it devolved to appoint the resting-place for the night. English Version suits the context best. <div eID="gen19277" type="x-p"/>

entries.a3165a23cc0c5cca80b48423d2e3fbdfb208c3b1: <div eID="gen30743" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30744" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30745" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30745" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30744" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30746" type="x-p"/> Sequel of the prophecies of Jeremiah against Babylon. The dreadful, sudden, and final ruin that shall fall upon the Chaldeans, who have compelled the nations to receive their idolatrous rites, (see an instance in the third chapter of Daniel), set forth by a variety of beautiful figures; with a command to the people of God, (who have made continual intercession for the conversion of their heathen rulers), to flee from the impending vengeance, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1-Jer.51.14">Jer 51:1-14</reference>. Jehovah, Israel's God, whose infinite power, wisdom and understanding are every where visible in the works of creation, elegantly contrasted with the utterly contemptible objects of the Chaldean worship, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15-Jer.51.19">Jer 51:15-19</reference>. Because of their great oppression of God's people, the Babylonians shall be visited with cruel enemies from the north, whose innumerable hosts shall fill the land, and utterly extirpate the original inhabitants, vv. 20-44. One of the figures by which this formidable invasion is represented is awfully sublime. "The Sea is come up upon Babylon; she is covered with the multitude of the waves thereof." And the account of the sudden desolation produced by this great armament of a multitude of nations, (which the prophet, dropping the figure, immediately subjoins), is deeply afflictive. "Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness; a land wherein no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man pass thereby." The people of God a third time admonished to escape from Babylon, lest they be overtaken with her plagues, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.45">Jer 51:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.46">Jer 51:46</reference>. Other figures setting forth in a variety of lights the awful judgments with which the Chaldeans shall be visited on account of their very gross idolatries, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.47-Jer.51.58">Jer 51:47-58</reference>. The significant emblem with which the chapter concludes, of Seraiah, after having read the book of the Prophet Jeremiah against Babylon, binding a stone to it, and casting it into the river Euphrates, thereby prefiguring the very sudden downfall of the Chaldean city and empire, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59-Jer.51.64">Jer 51:59-64</reference>, is beautifully improved by the writer of the Apocalypse, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.21">Rev 18:21</reference>, in speaking of Babylon the Great, of which the other was a most expressive type; and to which many of the passages interspersed throughout the Old Testament Scriptures relative to Babylon must be ultimately referred, if we would give an interpretation in every respect equal to the terrible import of the language in which these prophecies are conceived. <div eID="gen30746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30748" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord - This chapter is a continuation of the preceding prophecy. <div eID="gen30748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30749" type="x-p"/> A destroying wind - Such as the pestilential winds in the east; and here the emblem of a destroying army, carrying all before them, and wasting with fire and sword.
entries.77465b353097be0418c975a9ff192e330200a427: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30750" type="x-p"/> And will send - fanners - When the corn is trodden out with the feet of cattle, or crushed out with a heavy wheel armed with iron, with a shovel they throw it up against the wind, that the chaff and broken straw may be separated from it. This is the image used by the prophet; these people shall be trodden, crushed, and fanned by their enemies.
entries.1ae69120dfe8e093f98c8b2bc0f6c875f92c9ed2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30751" type="x-p"/> For Israel hath not been forsaken - God still continued his prophets among them; he had never cast them wholly off. Even in the midst of wrath - highly deserved and inflicted punishment, he has remembered mercy; and is now about to crown what he has done by restoring them to their own land. I conceive אשם asham, which we translate sin, as rather signifying punishment, which meaning it often has.
entries.0d03dc81700d6d5bba5a7d6261dc295467008c53: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30752" type="x-p"/> Made all the earth drunken - The cup of God's wrath is the plenitude of punishment, that he inflicts on transgressors. It is represented as intoxicating and making them mad.
entries.b793e674eef25008179e170b68d17f40f7558302: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30753" type="x-p"/> Babylon is suddenly fallen and destroyed - These appear to be the words of some of the spectators of Babylon's misery.
entries.d010e662bd0b945407271462a368e1ca9c2cbe8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30754" type="x-p"/> We would have healed Babylon - Had it been in our power, we would have saved her; but we could not turn away the judgment of God.
entries.317d72bb332aeb99e51c6f5914752200e64ed68f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30755" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath brought forth our righteousness - This is the answer of the Jews. God has vindicated our cause.
entries.f5acd03a1fa4fbeaf4312aeb08e93001c70facab: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30756" type="x-p"/> Make bright the arrows - This is the prophet's address to Babylon. <div eID="gen30756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30757" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes - Of Cyaxares king of Media, called Darius the Mede in Scripture; and of Cyrus king of Persia, presumptive heir of the throne of Cyaxares, his uncle. Cambyses, his father, sent him, Cyrus, with 30, 000 men to assist his uncle Cyaxares, against Neriglissar king of Babylon, and by these was Babylon overthrown.
entries.9a02b0b5bebad2f62a40356731ebe0c8342fdda6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30758" type="x-p"/> Set up the standard - A call to the enemies of Babylon to invest the city and press the siege.
entries.82bd5249af401691573076873ed6013e9091ff17: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30759" type="x-p"/> O thou that dwellest upon many waters - Thou who hast an abundant supply of waters. It was built on the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates; the latter running through the city. But the many waters may mean the many nations which belonged to the Babylonish empire; nations and people are frequently so called in Scripture.
entries.1aa42320c373d58f94b66b37d07667e3a580f3d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> I will fill thee with men - By means of these very waters through the channel of thy boasted river, thou shalt be filled with men, suddenly appearing as an army of locusts; and, without being expected, shall lift up a terrific cry, as soon as they have risen from the channel of the river.
entries.affb8bd313ae0edda847928a901c53b63a397693: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> He hath made the earth by his power - The omnipotence of God is particularly manifested in the works of creation. <div eID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30762" type="x-p"/> He hath established the world by his wisdom - The omniscience of God is particularly seen in the government of תבל tebel, the inhabited surface of the globe. What a profusion of wisdom and skill is apparent in that wondrous system of providence by which he governs and provides for every living thing. <div eID="gen30762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30763" type="x-p"/> And hath stretched out the heaven by his understanding - Deep thought, comprehensive design, and consummate skill are especially seen in the formation, magnitudes, distances, revolutions, and various affections of the heavenly bodies.
entries.f9781cfb7264ca7452926078eef099b3ab10b8d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30764" type="x-p"/> When he uttereth his voice - Sends thunder. <div eID="gen30764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30765" type="x-p"/> There is a multitude of waters - For the electric spark, by decomposing atmospheric air, converts the hydrogen and oxygen gases, of which it is composed, into water; which falls down in the form of rain. <div eID="gen30765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30766" type="x-p"/> Causeth the vapours to ascend - He is the Author of that power of evaporation by which the water is rarified, and, being lighter than the air, ascends in form of vapor, forms clouds, and is ready to be sent down again to water the earth by the action of his lightnings, as before. And by those same lightnings, and the agency of heat in general, currents of air are formed, moving in various directions, which we call winds.
entries.d9bf37219f7e5e5c623ed9fa7e971a99a68a0228: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30767" type="x-p"/> Every man is brutish by his knowledge - He is brutish for want of real knowledge; and he is brutish when he acknowledges that an idol is any thing in the world. These verses, from fifteen to nineteen, are transcribed from <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12-Jer.10.16">Jer 10:12-16</reference>.
entries.db773c648ec5e6a18e1c5ee7f9454b532c243051: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30768" type="x-p"/> Thou art my battle axe - I believe Nebuchadnezzar is meant, who is called, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jer 50:23</reference>, the hammer of the whole earth. Others think the words are spoken of Cyrus. All the verbs are in the past tense: "With thee have I broken in pieces," etc., etc.
entries.a42fd0c658648e188f3fb91578b949c19e30e14b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30769" type="x-p"/> And I will render - The ו vau should be translated but, of which it has here the full power: "But I will render unto Babylon."
entries.7a42877c36b6025f18146e6998d222044cd39c71: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen30769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30770" type="x-p"/> O destroying mountain - An epithet which he applies to the Babylonish government; it is like a burning mountain, which, by vomiting continual streams of burning lava inundates and destroys all towns, villages fields, etc., in its vicinity. <div eID="gen30770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30771" type="x-p"/> And roll thee down from the rocks - I will tumble thee from the rocky base on which thou restest. The combustible matter in thy bowels being exhausted, thou shalt appear as an extinguished crater; and the stony mutter which thou castest out shall not be of sufficient substance to make a foundation stone for solidity, or a corner stone for beauty, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.26">Jer 51:26</reference>. Under this beautiful and most expressive metaphor, the prophet shows the nature of the Babylonish government; setting the nations on fire, deluging and destroying them by its troops, till at last, exhausted, it tumbles down, is extinguished, and leaves nothing as a basis to erect a new form of government on; but is altogether useless, like the cooled lava, which is, properly speaking, fit for no human purpose.
entries.55811075c787dd3fc16a50c7fd638d166c944f40: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30772" type="x-p"/> Set ye up a standard - Another summons to the Medes and Persians to attack Babylon. <div eID="gen30772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30773" type="x-p"/> Ararat, Minni - The Greater and Lesser Armenia. <div eID="gen30773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30774" type="x-p"/> And Ashchenaz - A part of Phrygia, near the Hellespont. So Bochart, Phaleg, lib. 1 c. 3, lib. 3 c. 9. Concerning Ashchenaz Homer seems to speak, Il. 2:370, 371: - Φορκυς αυ Φρυγας ηγε, και Ασκανιος θεοειδης, Τηλ' εξ Ασκανιης. "Ascanius, godlike youth, and Phorcys led <div eID="gen30774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30775" type="x-p"/> The Phrygians from Ascania's distant land." <div eID="gen30775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30776" type="x-p"/> Calmet thinks that the Ascantes, who dwelt in the vicinity of the Tanais, are meant.
entries.3601c8cbd8229d01f23b1ec7231552e238c30a5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen30776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30777" type="x-p"/> And the land shall tremble - It is represented here as trembling under the numerous armies that are passing over it, and the prancing of their horses.
entries.772794f3fa94bb1cf2c31211da66f2658518321c: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen30777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30778" type="x-p"/> The mighty men - have forborne to fight - They were panic-struck when they found the Medes and Persians within their walls, and at once saw that resistance was useless.
entries.7559929a2e5cbb53c0e3f757ec452ae4c6dc3bfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen30778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30779" type="x-p"/> One post shall run to meet another - As the city was taken by surprise, in the manner already related, so now messengers, one after another, were dispatched to give the king information of what was done; viz., that the city was taken at one end. Herodotus tells us that the extreme parts of the city were taken, before those of the center knew any thing of the invasion. Herodot. lib. 1 c. 191.
entries.be22b4c89ec1ad4c100e14d9cd6defdcf924b3be: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30780" type="x-p"/> That the passages are stopped - Either the bridges or slips for boats, by which the inhabitants passed from one side to the other, and may mean the principal gates or passes in the city, which the victorious army would immediately seize, that they might prevent all communication between the inhabitants. <div eID="gen30780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30781" type="x-p"/> The reeds they have burned with fire - What this means I cannot tell, unless it refer to something done after the taking of the city. Setting fire to the reeds in the marshy ground, in order the better to clear the places, and give a freer passage to the water, that it may neither stagnate nor turn the solid ground into a marsh. Dr. Blayney thinks it refers to the firing of the houses, in order to throw the inhabitants into the greater confusion; but no historian makes any mention of burning the city, except what is said <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">Jer 51:30</reference>, "They have burned her dwelling places;" and this may be a poetical expression. That they burnt nothing before they took the city must be evident from the circumstance of their taking the city by surprise, in the night time, with the greatest secrecy. Still there might have been some gates, barricadoes, or wooden works, serving for barracks or such like, which obstructed some of the great passages, which, when they had entered, they were obliged to burn, in order to get themselves a ready passage through the city. This is the more likely because this burning of reeds is connected with the stopping of the passages, burning the dwelling places, and breaking the bars.
entries.b91366608ab86dc35708de6d05087ee62a85af60: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen30781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30782" type="x-p"/> The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor - The threshing wheel is gone over her; she is trodden under foot.
entries.b9de5b38e0804301ffce3aa6b1f1b19e15558a94: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen30782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30783" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadrezzar - hath devoured me - These are the words of Judea; he has taken away all my riches. <div eID="gen30783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30784" type="x-p"/> He hath cast me out - He shall vomit all up; i.e., they shall be regained.
entries.4dfeba4a4471a861691335b119b9c7a8f6a7e05d: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen30784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30785" type="x-p"/> The violence done to me - be upon Babylon, - and my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea - Zion begins to speak, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jer 51:34</reference>, and ends with this verse. The answer of Jehovah begins with the next verse. Though the Chaldeans have been the instrument of God to punish the Jews, yet in return they, being themselves exceedingly wicked, shall suffer for all the carnage they have made, and for all the blood they have shed.
entries.5717d6e1a7dbd0b73d2a48de6cea6734874b768f: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen30785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30786" type="x-p"/> I will dry up her sea - Exhaust all her treasures.
entries.13e066e465efe609bbb6d73ebe19e60ebbec25d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen30786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30787" type="x-p"/> Without an inhabitant - See <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">Jer 50:39</reference>.
entries.7bae974fe98f1be89ed3b0ca27b268006240c701: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen30787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30788" type="x-p"/> In their heat I will make their feasts - It was on the night of a feast day, while their hearts were heated with wine and revelry, that Babylon was taken; see <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.3">Dan 5:1-3</reference>. This feast was held in honor of the goddess Sheshach, (or perhaps of Bel), who is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jer 51:41</reference>, as being taken with her worshippers. As it was in the night the city was taken, many had retired to rest, and never awoke; slain in their beds, they slept a perpetual sleep.
entries.2b785b3fe9596b0ae9d7f2f6094f67b696cf4b29: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen30788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30789" type="x-p"/> How is Sheshach taken! - Perhaps the city is here called by the name of its idol. <div eID="gen30789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30790" type="x-p"/> The praise of the whole earth - One of the seven wonders of the world; superexcellent for the height, breadth, and compass of its walls, its hanging gardens, the temple of Belus, etc., etc.
entries.e01b16ecbfc4461cc59197f26abb906ee1280a54: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen30790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30791" type="x-p"/> The sea is come up - A multitude of foes have inundated the city.
entries.05560cb76928124fb9270ea4654a57218fc4787a: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen30791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30792" type="x-p"/> I will punish Bel in Babylon - Bel or Belus was their supreme deity. <div eID="gen30792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30793" type="x-p"/> That which he hath swallowed up - The sacred vessels of the temple of Jerusalem, which were taken thence by Nebuchadnezzar, and dedicated to him in his temple at Babylon. <div eID="gen30793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30794" type="x-p"/> The wall of Babylon shall fall - It shall cease to be a defense; and shall moulder away until, in process of time, it shall not be discernible.
entries.18e0abfe1e541a60830d68a2817d5a9e6af2f588: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen30794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30795" type="x-p"/> My people, go ye out - A warning to all the Jews in Babylon to leave the city, and escape for their lives.
entries.380f1dd7349c304739b93f6f2c22fb0fd0c7af72: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen30795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30796" type="x-p"/> A rumor shall - come one year - A year before the capture of the city there shall be a rumor of war, - and in that year Belshazzar was defeated by Cyrus. In the following year the city was taken.
entries.b7fcd8de60c3e7ba30d77c161db57917c544d431: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen30796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30797" type="x-p"/> The heaven and the earth - shall sing for Babylon - Its fall shall be a subject of universal rejoicing.
entries.ffe8750a5afab19366b6cd5a0db2e98d18f6fe31: <hi type="bold">Verse 50</hi> <div eID="gen30797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30798" type="x-p"/> Ye that have escaped the sword - The Jews. <div eID="gen30798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30799" type="x-p"/> Let Jerusalem come into your mind - Pray for its restoration; and embrace the first opportunity offered of returning thither.
entries.a9c0629f2b4d4ab1e0aac504ef3d8c7060ba98f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen30799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30800" type="x-p"/> Strangers are come into the sanctuaries - The lamentation of the pious Jews for the profanation of the temple by the Chaldeans.
entries.2357f69a20b8af488cf525bbc602deb0d922035c: <hi type="bold">Verse 53</hi> <div eID="gen30800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30801" type="x-p"/> Though Babylon should mount up to heaven - Though it were fortified even to the skies, it shall fall by the enemies that I will send against it.
entries.d24385be604a3df96309bb6cf03783175cbdeef5: <hi type="bold">Verse 55</hi> <div eID="gen30801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30802" type="x-p"/> The great voice - Its pride and insufferable boasting.
entries.abda564224d216eedee6a76e6988be46e0c0ee5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 56</hi> <div eID="gen30802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30803" type="x-p"/> The Lord God of recompenses - The fall of Babylon is an act of Divine justice; whatever it suffers, it is in consequence of its crimes.
entries.02643fc5895d710e21244025ae1e3effea89759f: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen30803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30804" type="x-p"/> I will make drunk her princes - See on <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jer 51:39</reference> (note).
entries.ec544e7b5e086d7e9a3faa2d62b93ddec4aabe55: <hi type="bold">Verse 58</hi> <div eID="gen30804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30805" type="x-p"/> The broad walls of Babylon - Herodotus, who saw these walls, says, "The city was a regular square, each side of which was one hand red and twenty stadia, the circumference four hundred and eighty stadia. It was surrounded by a wall fifty cubits broad, and two hundred cubits high; and each side had twenty-five brazen gates." - Herod. lib. 1 c. 178. Had not Cyrus resorted to stratagem, humanly speaking, he could not have taken this city. For the destruction of this wall and its very vestiges, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Isa 13:19</reference> (note).
entries.9991f296804df38455c97d9a9b516fc01d94b39a: <hi type="bold">Verse 59</hi> <div eID="gen30805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30806" type="x-p"/> The word which Jeremiah - On account of the message sent by Jeremiah to the Jewish captives in Babylon.
entries.dc9a72b62a51b5e6ed24522f1a306d9bd50e4bf5: <hi type="bold">Verse 60</hi> <div eID="gen30806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30807" type="x-p"/> Wrote in a book - Whether this book contained any more than is recorded in this place we do not know; probably it contained no more than what is found in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.62-Jer.51.64">Jer 51:62-64</reference>. A book, ספר sepher, signifies, in Hebrew, any writing, great or small.
entries.7dc8d8bb29e67aaa98c8381c21881e1ad684f880: <hi type="bold">Verse 64</hi> <div eID="gen30807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30808" type="x-p"/> Thus shall Babylon sink, etc. - This is the emblem of its overthrow and irretrievable ruin. See <reference osisRef="Rev.18.21">Rev 18:21</reference>, where we find that this is an emblem of the total ruin of mystical Babylon. <div eID="gen30808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30809" type="x-p"/> Herodotus relates a similar action of the Phocaeans, who, having resolved to leave their country, and never return to it again, μυδρον σιδηρεον κατεπονωσαν, και ωμοσαν μη πριν ες Φωκαιην ἡξειν, πριν η τον μυδρον τουτον αναφηναι· "threw a mass of iron into the sea, and swore that they would never return to Phocaea till that iron mass should rise and swim on the top." The story is this: The Phocaeans, being besieged by Harpagus, general of the Persians, demanded one day's truce to deliberate on the propositions he had made to them relative to their surrendering their city; and begged that in the mean while he would take off his army from the walls. Harpagus having consented, they carried their wives, children, and their most valuable effects, aboard their ships; then, throwing a mass of iron into the sea, bound themselves by an oath never to return till that iron should rise to the top and swim. See Herodotus, lib. 1 c. 165. <div eID="gen30809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30810" type="x-p"/> Horace refers to this in his epode Ad Populum Romanum, Epode 16 ver. 25: - <div eID="gen30810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30811" type="x-p"/> Sed juremus in haec: simul imis saxa renarint <div eID="gen30811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30812" type="x-p"/> Vadis levata, ne redire sit nefas. "As the Phocaeans oft for freedom bled, <div eID="gen30812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30813" type="x-p"/> At length with imprecated curses fled." <div eID="gen30813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30814" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen30814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30815" type="x-p"/> Thus far are the words of Jeremiah - It appears that the following chapter is not the work of this prophet: it is not his style. The author of it writes Jehoiachin; Jeremiah writes him always Jeconiah, or Coniah. It is merely historical, and is very similar to 2 Kings 24:18-25:30. The author, whoever he was, relates the capture of Jerusalem, the fate of Zedekiah, the pillage and burning of the city and the temple. He mentions also certain persons of distinction who were slain by the Chaldeans. He mentions the number of the captives that were carried to Babylon at three different times; and concludes with the deliverance of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon, in which he had been for thirty-seven years. It is very likely that the whole chapter has been compiled from some chronicle of that time, or it was designed as a preface to the Book of the Lamentations; and would stand with great propriety before it, as it contains the facts on which that inimitable poem is built. Were it allowable, I would remove it to that place.  <chapter eID="Jer.51"/> <div eID="gen30815" type="x-p"/>

entries.8dc95b436cea5c0256c37cafad0eeaa12c87d3f3: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1-Jer.51.2">Jer 51:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1-Jer.51.4">Jer 51:1-4</reference>, the terrible character of the hostile nation is further described. Against Babylon and the inhabitants of Chaldea, God stirs up the "spirit of a destroyer," viz., a savage nation that will massacre the Chaldeans without pity. לב , lit., "the heart of mine adversaries," is the word כּשׂדּים, changed, according to the canon <hi type="italic">Atbash</hi> (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer 25:26</reference>), for the purpose of obtaining the important meaning that Chaldea is the centre of God’s enemies. This explanation of the name involves the thought that all enmity against God the Lord culminates in Babylon; on the basis of this representation Babylon is called, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.5">Rev 17:5</reference>, "the mother of harlots and abominations of the earth." רוּח משׁחית does not mean καύσωνα διαφθείροντα (lxx), <hi type="italic">ventum pestilentem</hi> (Vulgate), "a sharp wind" (Luther), nor, as it is usually translated, "a destroying wind;" for העיר רוּח is nowhere used of the rousing of a wind, but everywhere means "to rouse the spirit of any one," to stir him up to an undertaking; cf. Hag 1:14; <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.26">1Ch 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>, and 2Ch 36:22. Jeremiah also employs it thus in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jer 51:11</reference>, and this meaning is quite suitable here also. משׁחית is a substantive, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jer 4:7</reference> : "the spirit of a destroyer." The figure of winnowing, which follows in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.2">Jer 51:2</reference>, does not by any means necessarily require the meaning "wind," because the figure contained in the word זרוּה was first called forth by the employment of זרים, "strangers" = barbarians. The sending of the זרים to Babylon has no connection with the figure of the wind, and it even remains a question whether זרוּה really means here to winnow, because the word is often used of the scattering of a nation, without any reference to the figure of winnowing; cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Lev 26:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Eze 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.15">Eze 12:15</reference>, etc., also <reference osisRef="Jer.49.32">Jer 49:32</reference>, Jer 49:36. However, this thought is suggested by what follows, "they empty her hand," although the clause which assigns the reason, "because they are against her round about" (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.17">Jer 4:17</reference>), does not correspond with this figure, but merely declares that the enemies which attack Babylon on every side disperse its inhabitants and empty the land.
entries.6fd6be78c98e2330c237e5ab581f2a9f391b22cb: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.3-Jer.51.4">Jer 51:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> These strangers shall kill, without sparing, every warrior of Babylon, and annihilate its whole military forces. In the first half of the verse the reading is doubtful, since the Masoretes would have the second ידרד (<hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>) expunged, probably because (as Böttcher, <hi type="italic">N. Aehrenl</hi>. ii. S. 166, supposes) they considered it merely a repetition. The meaning is not thereby changed. According to the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>, we would require to translate, "against him who bends the bow, may there be, or come, one who bends his bow;" according to the <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi>, "against him who bends the bow, may he who bends his bow bend it." As to אל־ידרך with אשׁר omitted, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.12">1Ch 15:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.4">2Ch 1:4</reference>, and Ewald, §333, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. יתעל בּס' stands in apposition to אל־ידרך ; יתעל is the Hithpael from עלה, and means to raise oneself: it is to be taken as the shortened form of the imperfect passive; cf. Gesenius, §128, Rem. 2. Certainly, the Hithpael of עלה occurs nowhere else, but it is quite appropriate here; so that it is unnecessary, with Hitzig, to adduce, for explanation, the Arabic <hi type="italic">tl'</hi>, to stretch the head out of anything, or, with Ewald, to derive the form from the Aramaic עלל, Arabic <hi type="italic">gl</hi>, to thrust in. Neither is there any foundation for the remark, that the abbreviated form of the imperfect would be admissible only if אל were found instead of אל. Indeed, the Syriac, Targum, and Vulgate have actually read and rendered from אל, which several codices also present, "Let him not bend his bow, nor stretch himself in his coat of mail." But by this reading the first half of the verse is put in contradiction to the second; and this contradiction is not removed by the supposition of J. D. Michaelis and Hitzig, who refer these clauses to the Chaldeans, and find the thought expressed in them, that the Chaldeans, through loss of courage, cannot set themselves for defence. For, in that case, we would be obliged, with Hitzig, to explain as spurious the words that follow, "and spare ye not her young men;" but for this there is no valid reason. As to החרימוּ, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jer 50:21</reference>, Jer 50:26. On <reference osisRef="Jer.51.4">Jer 51:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.30">Jer 50:30</reference> and Jer 49:26. The suffix in "her streets" refers to Babylon.
entries.2225798e009b2e9f60695085e9a56e1a4c5aecf4: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5-Jer.51.14">Jer 51:5-14</reference> <div eID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> Because of the righteousness of Israel, Babylon is to be irretrievably destroyed. Jer 51:5. <hi type="italic">"For Israel is not forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of Jahveh of hosts; but their land is full of guilt because of the Holy One of Israel. </hi> Jer 51:6. <hi type="italic">Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save ye every one his life: do not perish for her iniquity; because it is a time of vengeance for Jahveh; He renders to her what she has committed. </hi> Jer 51:7. <hi type="italic">Babylon [was] a golden cup in the hand of Jahveh, that intoxicated all the earth. Nations have drunk of her wine, therefore nations are mad. </hi> Jer 51:8. <hi type="italic">Babylon has fallen suddenly and been broken: howl over her: take balsam for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. </hi> Jer 51:9. <hi type="italic">'We have tried to heal Babylon, but she is not healed. Leave her, and let us go each one to his own land; for her judgment reaches unto heaven, and is lifted up to the clouds.' </hi> Jer 51:10. <hi type="italic">Jahveh hath brought forth our righteousnesses; come, and let us declare in Zion the doing of Jahveh our God. </hi> Jer 51:11. <hi type="italic">Sharpen the arrow, fill the shields: Jahveh hath roused the spirit of the kings of Media; for His counsel is against Babylon, to destroy it; because it is the vengeance of Jahveh, the vengeance of His temple. </hi> Jer 51:12. <hi type="italic">Against the walls of Babylon raise a standard; strengthen the watch, set watchmen, prepare the ambushes: for Jahveh hath both devised and done what He spake against the inhabitants of Babylon. </hi> Jer 51:13. <hi type="italic">O thou that dwellest upon many waters, rich in treasures, thine end hath sworn by Himself, 'Surely I have filled thee with men, as [with] the locust; and they shall raise a shout of joy against thee.'"</hi> <div eID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14475" type="x-p"/> The offence of Babylon against the Holy One of Israel demands its destruction. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5">Jer 51:5</reference>, two reasons are given for God’s determination to destroy Babylon. The Lord is induced to this (1) by His relation to Israel and Judah, whom Babylon will not let go; (2) by the grave offence of Babylon. Israel is לא אלמן, "not widowed," forsaken by his God; i.e., Jahveh, the God of hosts, has not rejected His people for ever, so as not to trouble Himself any more about them; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>; Isa 54:4. "Their land" - the land of the Chaldeans - "is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel," partly through their relation to Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jer 50:21</reference>), partly through their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference>, 38). מן does not mean here "on the side of," but "on account of," because they do not acknowledge Jahveh as the Holy One of Israel.
entries.63b87137d0f45e082608e641baef8a4e849b8675: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15-Jer.51.26">Jer 51:15-26</reference> <div eID="gen14481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> The omnipotence of the Lord and Creator of the whole world will destroy the idols of Babylon, and break the mighty kingdom that rules the world. Jer 51:15. <hi type="italic">"He who made the earth by His strength, establishing the world by His wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by His understanding; </hi> Jer 51:16. <hi type="italic">When, thundering, He makes a roaring sound of water in the heavens, He causes clouds to ascend from the end of the earth, makes lightnings for the rain, and brings forth the wind out of His treasures. </hi> Jer 51:17. <hi type="italic">Every man without knowledge is brutish; every goldsmith is ashamed because of the image: for his molten work is a lie, and there is no spirit in them. </hi> Jer 51:18. <hi type="italic">They are vanity, a work of mockery; in their time of visitation they perish. </hi> Jer 51:19. <hi type="italic">The Portion of Jacob is not like these; for He is the framer of all, and of the tribe of his inheritance: Jahveh of hosts is His name. </hi> Jer 51:20. <hi type="italic">Thou art a hammer to me, weapons of war; and with thee I will break nations in pieces, and with thee destroy kingdoms. </hi> Jer 51:21. <hi type="italic">And with thee I will break in pieces the horse and his rider, and with thee I will break in pieces the chariot and its rider. </hi> Jer 51:22. <hi type="italic">And with thee I will break in pieces man and woman, and with thee I will break in pieces old and young, and with thee I will break in pieces young man and maiden. </hi> Jer 51:23. <hi type="italic">And with thee I will break in pieces the shepherd and his flock, and with thee I will break in pieces the husbandman and his yoke [of oxen], and with thee I will break in pieces governors and deputy-governors. </hi> Jer 51:24. <hi type="italic">And I will recompense to Babylon, and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea, all their evil which they have done in Zion before your eyes, saith Jahveh. </hi> Jer 51:25. <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee, O mountain of destruction, saith Jahve, that destroyed all the earth; and I will stretch out my hand against thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, and make thee a burnt mountain, </hi> Jer 51:26. <hi type="italic">So that they shall not take from thee a stone for a corner, or a stone for foundations; but thou shalt be desolations for ever, saith Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> In order to establish, against all doubt, the fall of Babylon that has been announced under solemn oath, Jeremiah, in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15">Jer 51:15</reference>-19. repeats a passage from the address in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12-Jer.10.16">Jer 10:12-16</reference>, in which he holds up before the people, by way of warning, the almighty power of the living God, and the destruction of the idols at the time of the judgment. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.10">Jer 51:10</reference> he wished, by means of this announcement, to combat the fears of the idolatrous people for the power of the heathen gods; here he seeks by the same means to destroy the confidence of the Chaldeans in their gods, and to state that all idols will be destroyed before the almighty power of the Creator and Ruler of the whole world on the day of judgment, and Israel shall then learn that He who formed the universe will show Himself, by the fall of Babylon, as the Creator of Israel. The whole passage is repeated verbatim, on till a change made in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.19">Jer 51:19</reference>, where ישׂראל is omitted before שׁבט נחלתו, and these words are connected with what precedes: "He is the former of all, and of the tribe which belongs to Him as His own property," i.e., Israel. This alteration is not to be put to the account of a copyist, who omitted the word "Israel" through an oversight, but is due to Jeremiah: there was no need here, as in Jer 10, for bringing into special prominence the relation of Israel to his God.<note placement="foot">In <reference osisRef="Jer.10.16">Jer 10:16</reference> the lxx have taken no account either of ישׂראל or שׁבט. Hence Movers, Hitzig, and Ewald infer that these words have found their way into the text as a gloss suggested by <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>, and should be deleted. But in this they are wrong. The omission of the two words by the lxx is a result of the erroneous translation there given of the first clause of the verse. This the lxx have rendered ου ̓ τοιαύτη μερὶς τῷ  ̓Ιακωβ, instead of ου ̓ τοιαύτη ἡ μερὶς τοῦ  ̓Ιακώβ. Having done so, it was impossible for them to continue, ὅτι ὁ πλάσας τὰ πάντα αὐτός, because they could not predicate this of μερίς, which they evidently did not take to mean God. And if they were to connect הוּא with what followed, they were bound to omit the two words, for it would never have done to take together הוּא וישׂראל שׁבט נחלתו. They therefore simply omitted the troublesome words, and went on to translate: ὅτι ὁ πλάσας τὰ πάντα αὐτός κληρονομία αὐτοῦ. Cf. Nägelsbach. <hi type="italic">Jeremia u. Babylon</hi>, S. 94.</note> <div eID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> As to the rest, see the exposition of <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12">Jer 10:12</reference>-16. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20-Jer.51.26">Jer 51:20-26</reference> the destruction of Babylon and its power is further carried out in two figures. In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20-Jer.51.24">Jer 51:20-24</reference> Babylon is compared to a hammer, which God uses for the purpose of beating to pieces nations and kingdoms, with their forces and their inhabitants, but on which He will afterwards requite the evil done to Zion. מפּץ is equivalent to מפיץ ot tnelaviuqe si, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">Pro 25:18</reference>, one who breaks in pieces; hence a battle-hammer. Hitzig takes כּלי to be a singular, "formed thus in order to avoid an accumulation of <hi type="italic">i</hi> sounds (cf. פּליטים with פּליטי)." This is possible, but neither necessary nor probable. The plural, "weapons of war," is added, because the battle-hammer is considered as including all weapons of war. By the hammer, Ewald understands "the true Israel;" Hitzig, Cyrus, the destroyer of Babylon; Nägelsbach, an ideal person. These three views are based on the fact that the operation performed by means of the hammer (breaking to pieces) is marked by perfects with ו <hi type="italic">relative</hi> (ונפּצתּי), which is also true of the retribution to be made on Babylon: from this it is inferred that the breaking with the hammer, as well as the retribution, is still future, and that the meaning is, "When I hammer in this way with thee, I will requite Babylon" (Hitzig); while Ewald concludes from nothing but the context that the words refer to Israel. <div eID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> But none of these reasons is decisive, nor any of the three views tenable. The context gives decided support to the opinion that in Jer 51:20. it is Babylon that is addressed, just as in Jer 51:13. and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jer 51:25</reference>; a further proof is, that as early as <reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jer 50:23</reference>, Babylon is called "the hammer of the whole earth." Only very weighty reasons, then, could induce us to refer the same figure, as used here, to another nation. The word פּטּישׁ (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jer 50:23</reference>), "hammer, smith’s hammer" (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.7">Isa 41:7</reference>), is not essentially different from מפּץ, which is used here. The figure is quite inapplicable to Israel, because "Israel is certainly to be delivered through the destruction of Babylon, but is not to be himself the instrument of the destruction" (Graf). Finally, the employment of the perfect with w relative, both in connection with the shattering to pieces which God accomplishes with (by means of) Babylon, and also the retribution He will execute on Babylon, is explained by the fact, that just as, in prophetic vision, what Babylon does to the nations, and what happens to it, was not separated into two acts, distinct from one another, but appeared as one continuous whole, so also the work of Babylon as the instrument of destruction was not yet finished, but had only begun, and still continuing, was partly future, like the retribution which it was to receive for its offence against Zion; just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jer 51:13</reference> Babylon is viewed as then still in the active exercise of its power; and the purpose for which God employs it, as well as the fate that is to befall it, is presented together in something like this manner: "O Babylon, who art my hammer with which I break peoples and kingdoms in pieces, thee will I requite!" There is separate mention made of the instances of breaking, in a long enumeration, which becomes tedious through the constant repetition of the verb - something like the enumeration in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.35-Jer.50.38">Jer 50:35-38</reference>, where, however, the constant repetition of חרב gives great emphasis to the address. First comes the general designation, nations and kingdoms; then military forces; then (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jer 51:25</reference>) the inhabitants of the kingdoms, arranged, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">Eze 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">Eze 23:23</reference>, according to sex, age, and class, labouring classes (shepherds, and husbandmen with their cattle); and lastly dignitaries, satraps and lieutenant-governors, פּחות וּסגנים, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">Eze 23:6</reference>, Eze 23:23. פּחה probably comes from the Zendic <hi type="italic">pavan</hi> (root <hi type="italic">pa</hi>), of which a dialectic form is <hi type="italic">pagvan</hi>, "upholder of government;" see on Hag 1:1. סגן corresponds to the ζωγάνης of the Athenians, "lieutenant-governor;" but it is not much that has hitherto been ascertained with regard to this office; see Delitzsch on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.25">Isa 41:25</reference> Clark’s translation. On 'ושׁלּמתּי וגו, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">Jer 51:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">Jer 50:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference>; "before your eyes," towards the end of this verse, belongs to this verb in the main clause. <div eID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14486" type="x-p"/> This retribution is set forth in Jer 51:25. under a new figure. Babylon is called the "mountain of destruction;" this name is immediately explained by the predicate, "that destroys the whole earth," brings destruction on it. The name הר המשׁחית is applied in 2Ki 23:13 to the Mount of Olives, or its southern summit, the so-called <hi type="italic">mons offensionis vel scandali</hi> of ecclesiastical tradition, on which Solomon had erected idolatrous altars for his foreign wives; the name refers to the pernicious influence thereby exercised on the religious life of Israel. In this verse, "destruction" is used in a comprehensive sense of the physical and moral ruin which Babylon brought on the nations. Babylon is a "mountain," as being a powerful kingdom, supereminent above others; whether there is also a reference in the title to its lofty buildings (C. B. Michaelis) seems doubtful. "I will roll thee down from the rocks," <hi type="italic">de petris, in quarum fastigiis hucusque eminuisti. Non efferes te amplius super alia regna</hi> (C. B. Mich.). To this Hitzig adds, by way of explanation: "The summit of the mountain is sometimes changed into the very position occupied by the crater." From what follows, "I will make thee a mountain of burning," i.e., either a burning, or burnt, burnt-out mountain, modern expositors infer, with J. D. Michaelis, that the prophet has before his mind a volcano in active eruption, "for no other kind of mountains could devastate countries; it is just volcanoes which have been hollowed out by fire that fall in, or, it may be, tumble down into the valley below, scattering their constituent elements here and there; the stones of such mountains, too, are commonly so much broken and burnt, that they are of no use for building" (Hitzig). Of the above remarks this much is correct, that the words, "I will make thee a burning mountain," are founded on the conception of a volcano; any more extended application, however, of the figure to the whole verse is unwarranted. The clause, "I will roll thee down from the rocks," cannot possibly be applied to the action of a volcano in eruption (though Nägelsbach does so apply it), unless we are ready to impute to the prophet a false notion regarding the eruptions of volcanoes. By the eruption, a mountain is not loosened from the rock on which it rests, and hurled down into the valleys round about; it is only the heart of the mountain, or the rocks on which its summit rests, that seem to be vomited out of it. Besides, the notion that there is a representation of an active volcano in the first clauses of the verse, is disproved by the very fact that the mountain, Babylon, does not bring ruin on the earth, as one that is burning; it is not to become such until after it has been rolled down from the rocks on which it rests. The laying waste of the countries is not ascribed to the fire that issues from the mountain, but the mountain begins to burn only after it has been rolled down from its rocks. Babylon, as a kingdom and city, is called a mountain, because it mightily surpassed and held sway over them; cf. Isa 2:14. It brings ruin on the whole earth by subjugation of the nations and devastation of the countries. The mountain rests on rocks, i.e., its power has a foundation as firm as a rock, until the Lord rolls it down from its height, and burns the strong mountain, making it like an extinct volcano, the stones of which, having been rendered vitreous by the fire, no longer furnish material that can be employed for the foundation of new buildings. "A corner-stone," etc., is explained by C. B. Michaelis, after the Chaldee, Kimchi, and others, to mean, "no one will appoint a king or a prince any more out of the stock of the Chaldeans." This is against the context, according to which the point treated of is, not the fall of the kingdom in or of Babylon, but the destruction of Babylon as a city and kingdom. Hitzig and Graf, accordingly, take the meaning to be this: Not a stone of the city will be used for a new building - no one will any more build for himself among their ruins, and out of the material there. The corner-stone and the foundation (it is further asserted) are mentioned by way of example, not because particularly large and good stones are needed for these parts, but because every house begins with them. But though the following clause, "thou shalt be an everlasting desolation," contains this idea, yet this interpretation neither exhausts nor gives a generally correct view of the meaning of the words, "no one will take from thee a corner-stone or a foundation-stone." The burning of the mountain signifies not merely that Babylon was to be burned to ashes, but that her sway over the world was to be quite at an end; this was only to come about when the city was burnt. When no stone of any value for a new building is to be left after this conflagration, this is equivalent to saying that nothing will be left of the empire that has been destroyed, which would be of any use in the foundation of another state. The last clause also ("for thou shalt be," etc.) refers to more than the destruction of the city of Babylon. This is seen even in the fundamental passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer 25:12</reference>, where the same threat is uttered against the land of the Chaldeans.
entries.25e152a54bdbe114202ae552993db51a09e631df: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27-Jer.51.28">Jer 51:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen14486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> A summons addressed to the nations to fight against Babylon, in order that, by reducing the city, vengeance may be taken for the offence committed against Israel by Babylon. Jer 51:27. <hi type="italic">"Lift up a standard on the earth, sound a trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, call the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz against her; appoint troops against her; bring up horses lie horrid locusts. </hi> Jer 51:28. <hi type="italic">Prepare nations against her, the kings of the Medes and her governors, and all her lieutenant-governors, and all the land of his dominion. </hi> Jer 51:29. <hi type="italic">Then the earth quakes and trembles: for the purposes of Jahveh against Babylon are being performed, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without an inhabitant. </hi> Jer 51:30. <hi type="italic">The heroes of Babylon have ceased to fight, they sit in the strongholds: their strength is dried up; they have become women; they have set her habitations on fire; her bars are broken. </hi> Jer 51:31. <hi type="italic">One runner runs against another, and one messenger against another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is wholly taken. </hi> Jer 51:32. <hi type="italic">And the crossing-places have been seized, and the marches have they burned up with fire, and the men of war are confounded. </hi> Jer 51:33. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing-floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little, and the time of harvest will come to her. </hi> Jer 51:34. <hi type="italic">Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured us, and ground us down; he hath set us down [like] an empty vessel, he hath swallowed us like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my dainties; he hath thrust me out. </hi> Jer 51:35. <hi type="italic">Let the inhabitress of Zion say, 'My wrong and my flesh [be] upon Babylon;' and let Jerusalem say, 'My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea.' </hi> Jer 51:36. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith Jahveh: Behold, I will plead thy cause, and execute vengeance for thee; ad I will dry up her sea, and make her fountain dry. </hi> Jer 51:37. <hi type="italic">And Babylon shall become heaps [of ruins], a dwelling-place of dragons, an astonishment, and a hissing, without an inhabitant."</hi> <div eID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> The lifting up of the standard (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jer 51:27</reference>) serves as a signal for the nations to assemble for the struggle against Babylon. בּארץ does not mean "in the land," but, as the parallel "among the nations" shows, "on the earth." קדּשׁוּ, "consecrate prepare against her (Babylon) nations" for the war; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">Jer 6:4</reference>; Jer 22:7. השׁמיעוּ, as in Jer 50:29. The kingdoms summoned are: <hi type="italic">Ararat</hi>, i.e., the middle (or eastern) province of Armenia, in the plain of Araxes, which Moses of Chorene calls Arairad, Araratia (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.8.4">Gen 8:4</reference>); <hi type="italic">Minni</hi>, which, according to the Syriac and Chaldee, is also a name of Armenia, probably its western province (see Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>, p. 807); and <hi type="italic">Ashkenaz</hi>, which the Jews take to be Germany, although only this much is certain, that it is a province in the neighbourhood of Armenia. For <hi type="italic">Askên</hi> is an Armenian proper name, and <hi type="italic">az</hi> an Armenian termination; cf. Lagarde’s <hi type="italic">Gesammelte Abhandll</hi>. S. 254, and Delitzsch on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.3">Gen 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.4">Gen 10:4</reference> ed. פּקדוּ, "appoint, order against her." טפסר does not mean "captains" or leaders, for this meaning of the foreign word (supposed to be Assyrian) rests on a very uncertain etymology; it means some peculiar kind of troops, but nothing more definite can be affirmed regarding it. This meaning is required by the context both here and in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>, the only other place where the word occurs: see on that passage. The sing. טפסר corresponds with the sing. סוּס, and is therefore to be taken collectively, "troops and horses." Whether the simile כּילק ס belongs merely to "horses," or to the combination "troops and horses," depends on the meaning attached to the expression. Modern expositors render it "bristly locusts;" and by that they understand, like Credner (<hi type="italic">Joel</hi>, S. 298), the young grasshopper after it has laid aside its third skin, when the wings are still enveloped in rough horny sheaths, and stick straight up from the back of the animal. But this explanation rests on an erroneous interpretation of Nah 3:17. סמר means to shudder, and is used of the shivering or quivering of the body (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Psa 119:120</reference>), and of the hair (<reference osisRef="Job.4.15">Job 4:15</reference>); and ילק does not mean a particular kind of locusts, through Jerome, on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Nah 3:17</reference>, renders it <hi type="italic">attelabus (parva locusta est inter locustam et bruchum, et modicis pennis reptans potius quam volans, semperque subsiliens)</hi>, but is a poetic epithet of the locust, "the devourer." If any one prefers to view סמר as referring to the nature of the locusts, he may with Bochart and Rosenmüller, think of the <hi type="italic">locustarum species, quae habet caput hirsutum</hi>. But the epithet "horrid" is probably intended merely to point out the locusts as a fearful scourge of the country. On this view, the comparison refers to both clauses, and is meant to set forth not merely the enormous multitude of the soldiery, but also the devastation they make of the country.
