But. we see that Jeremiah, when the kingdom had fallen, when the king with all his children was exposed to extreme disgrace, when in short the covenant of God seemed wholly abolished, still continued to discharge his office, which he certainly did not do in vain.<div eID="gen67753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67754" type="x-p"/>When, therefore, he understood that his teaching would not be without fruit, he was thus induced to speak first of God’s judgments; secondly, to exhort the people to repentance; thirdly, to encourage them to hope; and lastly, to open the door for prayer to God, so that the people in their extremities might venture to flee to God’s mercy; which could not have been done without faith.<div eID="gen67754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67755" type="x-p"/>We now in a measure understand for what purpose this Book was written by Jeremiah: his object was to shew that though nothing in the land appeared but desolation, and the Temple being destroyed, the Covenant of God appeared as made void, and thus all hope of salvation had been cut off, yet hope still remained, provided the people sought God in true repentance and faith; and he thus proceeded in the course of his calling, and made it evident that his doctrine would not be without benefit.<div eID="gen67755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67756" type="x-p"/>He indeed bewails, as I have said, the extreme calamity of his people; but he mingles with his lamentations the doctrine of repentance and faith’ For, on the one hand, he shews that the people suffered a just punishment for the many iniquities, of which they could not have been healed; and then, on the other hand, he gives them some intimations of God’s mercy, that in death itself the Jews might seek life, nay, that in the lowest depths they might know that God would be propitious to them. He at length by his own example stimulates them to pray; but prayer is founded on faith. It then follows, that Jeremiah, when the people had become wholly alienated from the worship of God, yet spent his labor in collecting together the remnant. Though, then, the whole Church was not only in the greatest disorder, but also reduced as it were almost to nothing, yet Jeremiah constructed some sort of building out of the ruins. This is the substance of this Book.<div eID="gen67756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67757" type="x-p"/>The Greek Translators call this Book <foreign xml:lang="el">Θρήνους</foreign>, Lamentations, and very properly, as also the Hebrews call it <foreign xml:lang="he">קינוה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">kinut</hi>; though the common name or title is <foreign xml:lang="he">אכה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">aike</hi>, from the first word in it. But when they wish to express what the Book contains, they call it <foreign xml:lang="he">קינות</foreign>, <hi type="italic">kinut</hi>, Lamentations.<div eID="gen67757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67758" type="x-p"/>Let us now proceed to the words; for what I have now briefly touched upon, can be more fully explained as we go on.<div eID="gen67758" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen67747"/> <div sID="gen67759"/> <div sID="gen67760" type="x-p"/>CHAPTER 1<div eID="gen67760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen67761"/> <div sID="gen67762" type="x-p"/>Lecture First.<div eID="gen67762" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen67761"/> <div sID="gen67763"/> <table> <row> <cell> <div sID="gen67764" type="x-p"/><reference osisRef="Bible:Lam.1.1">Lamentations 1:1</reference><div eID="gen67764" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen67765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> How doth the city sit solitary <hi type="italic">that was</hi> full of people! <hi type="italic">how</hi> is she become as a widow! she <hi type="italic">that was</hi> great among the nations, <hi type="italic">and</hi> princess among the provinces, <hi type="italic">how</hi> is she become tributary!<div eID="gen67765" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen67766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> Quomodo sedet solitaria civitas, quae abundavit populo! facta est tanquam vidua, quae magna fuit in gentibus! Quae dominataest in provinciis, redacta est ad tributum!<div eID="gen67766" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row> </table> <div sID="gen67767" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen67767" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="51" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. LI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against them that dwell in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>in the heart.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the midst of them that rise up against me, a destroying wind <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In this chapter the prophesie of the destruction of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is continued under new Metaphors, he begins with that of a Wind, a destroying Wind, (as northerly winds are ordinarily very pernicious,) but the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> idiom so ill suiteth that of other Languages that it is no easie matter positively to assert the sense of the words used. In the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> they are <ns0:hi>and to, or against those that inhabit the heart of those that rise up.</ns0:hi> Some would have it those that are wise in their own opinion and are there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore said to dwell in their heart. Others, those that are secure, but the best Interpreters judge our Translation to have best hit the sense,—<ns0:hi>them that dwell in the heart, i. e.</ns0:hi> that is in the midst of the <ns0:hi>Caldeans</ns0:hi> who are here said to have risen up against God, to strive against God, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 50.24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And will send unto Babylon <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 15.7.</ns0:note> fanners, that shall fan her, and empty her land <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Wicked men are compared to chaff, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2.4. Such as execute judgment on them are called <ns0:hi>fanners, Ier.</ns0:hi> 15.7. So <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 3.12. because as the fanner keepeth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> what is in the fan un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quiet in a continual motion and agitation, by which (advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />taged by the Wind) he emptieth it of the chaff: so the execu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioners of Gods vengeance, by a succession of judgments keeps a people from quiet, till all their chaff be winnowed out, and the fan be emptied of all but the more solid grain.</ns0:note>: for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For (he saith) as the fanner first ridleth what he hath in his fan one way, then another, first throweth it up, then lets it fall into the fan, so the Enemies should be round about <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and God would be on every side and every way destroying them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Against <ns0:hi>him that</ns0:hi> bendeth, let the archer bend his bow, and against <ns0:hi>him that</ns0:hi> lifteth up himself in his Brigandine <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">What ever Arms the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> shall be armed with, they shall meet with their matches, those that are Archers, shall meet with Archers to bend the Bow against them, and those who are otherwise armed shall meet with persons prepared to incounter them at their own weapons.</ns0:note>? and spare ye not her young men, destroy ye utterly all her host <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Their whole host shall be destroyed both young and old men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Thus the slain shall fall in the land of the Caldeans, and <ns0:hi>they that are</ns0:hi> thrust through <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 49.26.</ns0:note> in her streets <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thus all of them shall be destroyed, some in the Fields, some in the Streets of their Cities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For Israel <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>been</ns0:hi> forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of the LORD of hosts <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That is, not utterly forsaken, for in a sense they were for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saken as to some gradual manifestations of Gods love to them, but <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> were not left as a Widow, or were not di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vorced from God.</ns0:note>; though their land was filled with sin against the holy one of Israel <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The word translated sin signifies a most heinous sinning, or desolation and the best Interpreters judge that <ns0:hi>sin</ns0:hi> here signifieth the punishment of sin. God hath not forsaken the Jews utterly, though as they were formerly filled with grievous sins, so they be now filled with grievous judge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments because of their sins.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 18.4.</ns0:note> Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liver every man his own soul: be not cut off in her iniquity <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">It is a matter of no great moment whether we understand these words as spoken to the Jews in the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 50.8. or to those whom the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> had hired to help them. Or to such strangers as for their secular advantages lived in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Soul</ns0:hi> here seemeth to be meant <ns0:hi>Life,</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Iniquity</ns0:hi> the punishment of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> iniquity (as the <ns0:hi>Heb. word</ns0:hi> oft signifies) though in the New Testament these words be used as a monition to people to separat from the Idolatries of mystical <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> yet they seeth here to be onely a warning to others to remove out of the reach of <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> fall.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 50.15, 28.</ns0:note> this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the time of the LORDS vengeance, he will render unto her a re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />compence <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For the time is come when God hath determined to take vengeance on <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and to recompence to her all her sin, and that cruelty which she shewed to the Jews in particular.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Babylon <ns0:hi>hath been</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 14.8. and 17.4.</ns0:note> a golden cup in the LORDS hand, that made all the earth drunken <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">A <ns0:hi>golden Cup,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ause of her great riches and plenty, God hitherto had made use of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> as a rod in his hand, and had given her riches and power, and prosperity proportioned to the service he had for her to do, what she did she did by com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mission from God, therefore this golden cup is said to have been in the Lords hand, she had made all the nations about her drunken with the Lords fury.</ns0:note>: the nations have drunken of her wine, therefore the nations are mad <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Conquering them all, and making them mad through the misery and smart they felt from her. <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> is compared to an head of Gold, and <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.4, She is said to have had a golden cup in her hand, but the meaning is no more then this. That God had raised up <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> to great degrees of dignity and splendor intending to make use of her to execute his vengeance upon many other people, and he did accordingly so use her, to give the cup of his fury to many Nations to the enraging of divers people, but now the course of his Providence toward her was altering, &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Babylon is suddenly <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 21.9. Rev. 14.8. and 18.2.</ns0:note> fallen and destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That is, she shall suddenly fall and be destroyed, you may try all the probable wayes for her care, but they will all be used to no purpose.</ns0:note>: howl for her, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 46.11.</ns0:note> take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That is, she shall suddenly fall and be destroyed, you may try all the probable wayes for her cure, but they will all be used to no purpose.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:64" />9 We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The Prophet here seemeth to personate the merce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary Souldiers that should come to help the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> as if they should say this, they would have helped <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> but there was no healing for her.</ns0:note>, forsake her, and let us go every one to his own country <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And therefore they call one to another to leave her to her self, and return each man to his own Countrey.</ns0:note>, for her judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> to the skies <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For her punishment was very great, her case too sad for them to help. The reaching of things to the Heavens, and lifting them up to the skies are phrases used to signifie high and great measures, and degrees of things so ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 11.4. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 1.28. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 107.26.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 The LORD hath brought forth our righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness, come and let us <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 50.28.</ns0:note> declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">These words are spoken as in the person of the Jews own<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the destruction of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> to be the mighty work of God. 2. An act of justice and judgment pleading the cause and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venging the wrongs of his people and owning the Jewish Reli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gion, and calling one to another to go to the Temple to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clare what God had done for them, and to give thanks unto him for it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 46.4.</ns0:note> Make <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>pure.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> bright the arrows <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Prepare the Arrows for fighting, whether by feathering, sharpning<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or polishing and cleansing of them, is not much materi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al.</ns0:note>, gather the shields <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">You that are <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> gather all the Shields you have together, you will have need of them all: or you that are the Enemies of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> gather you together your Shields.</ns0:note>, the LORD hath <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 13.17.</ns0:note> raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">For God hath put a Spirit into <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Darius,</ns0:hi> &c. and his design is against <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> to destroy it.</ns0:note>, for his device <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> against Babylon to destroy it, because it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 50.28.</ns0:note> vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance of his temple <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">It is a day in which God is resolved to take vengeance on <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> to take vengeance for the indignities they have offered to, and the horrible profa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation of his Temple.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Set up the standard upon the walls of Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon, make the watch strong, set up the watchmen, prepare the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>liers in wait.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> ambushes <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Some judge these words spoken to the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> declaring the Will of God, that they should use all probable means to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quer <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> or (as some would have it) display their Banners upon the Walls of it, as signs of its being already conquered: but certainly it is more reasonable to conclude them the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets words to the <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> either rousing them out of their security (for it appears they were strangely secure from <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 5. Historians tell us that the City was fortified by Walls fifty cubits high, and 2 hundred cubits broad, and by a very deep and large ditch, besides that on one it had the River <ns0:hi>Euphrates</ns0:hi>) or at least quickening them to make all the preparation they could, though all would be to very little purpose, for God had resolved upon what he would do upon <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and it was already as good as done.</ns0:note>: for the LORD hath both devised and done that which he spake against the inhabitants of Babylon.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 O thou that dwellest upon many waters <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is said to dwell upon many waters because upon the great River <ns0:hi>Euphrates,</ns0:hi> which they say did not onely run by it, but almost incompass it, branching it self into many smaller Rivers which made several parts of the City, Islands.</ns0:note>, abundant in treasures <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It is a City much noted in Scripture for wealth, and made much more wealthy then it was by traffick by the conquest of many Nations.</ns0:note>, thine end is come, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the measure of thy covetousness <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Prophet tells them that now their gathering time was over, there was now a boundary set to their covetous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> it is the cubit of thy <ns0:hi>covetousness,</ns0:hi> which is by our translators well translated a <ns0:hi>measure,</ns0:hi> because it was amongst the Jews the common measure of height and depth. The word by us translated covetousness, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 18.21. may either sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifie <ns0:hi>riches</ns0:hi> the object of their covetousness, or prosperity, or that unlawful desire of having more which is properly called <ns0:hi>Covetousness,</ns0:hi> either because they should be destroyed utterly, or because they should prosper no more, there was no end put to the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> lusts, but there was an end put to the satisfaction of their lusts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 The LORD of hosts hath sworn by <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>his soul.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Lord that is able to bring to pass what he saith, hath sworn by his Life, or by himself, see the like phrase <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 45.23. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 22.5. & 44.26. & 49.13. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 4.2. & 6.8. that is the thing next mentioned shall come to pass as certainly as that there is a God in Heaven, or that God liveth.</ns0:note> Surely I will fill thee with men, as with caterpillars <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I will bring against thee a great Army, that shall be like a swarm of Cater<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pillars, and shall come against thee in such numbers as Cater<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pillars use to come, and for the same end to eat thee up, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy thee, and as Souldiers use to do when they go on to fight their Enemies, or to assault Cities, they shall make a great shout against thee.</ns0:note>; and they shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>utter.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> lift up a shout against thee <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1.1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 6. chap. 10, 12, 13.14, 15.</ns0:note> He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 9.8. Psal. 104.2. Isa. 40.22.</ns0:note> stretched out the heaven by his under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 When he uttereth <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> voice <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>noise.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> multitude of waters in the heavens, and he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 135.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth, he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sures.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 10.14.</ns0:note> Every man <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>is more brutish <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to know.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> is brutish by <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge, every founder is confounded by the gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven image: for his molten image <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> falshood, and <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no breath in them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 They <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> vanity, the work of errors: in the time of their visitation they shall perish.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 10.16.</ns0:note> The portion of Jacob <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not like them, for he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the former of all things, and <ns0:hi>Israel is</ns0:hi> the rod of his inheritance: the LORD of hosts <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> his name <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">We had these five verses all in the 10th. chapter, verse 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. See there the explication of the several passages in them, the scope of which is only to convince those to whom the Prophet spoke that notwithstanding all the pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er, and Riches, and Greatness, and Alliances of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> yet that God who had threatned this ruine to them was able to bring it upon them, and all their Idols were vanities, things of nought that should not be able to protect them, and from whose power or impotency, they must not measure nor make up a judgement of what God was able to do, for <ns0:hi>Israels</ns0:hi> God was that God who made the World, and the Lord of all the Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies of the Creatures whether in Heaven or Earth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 50.23.</ns0:note> Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> my battle-ax <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> weapons of war: for <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> thee</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>by thee.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doms <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Interpreters are here divided, whether by <ns0:hi>thou</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>thee</ns0:hi> in this and the following verses to understand <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> whom God made use of to destroy <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and many other places, or <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi> Our Translators understand it of <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> and therefore speak of the future tense, <ns0:hi>will I.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text will not resolve us; I rather incline to interpret it of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> as indeed the most do, and so it should be, <ns0:hi>Thou hast been,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>art,</ns0:hi> for that is the sense, <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Darius</ns0:hi> were not yet in being. God had made use of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> like an <ns0:hi>Hammer</ns0:hi> or Battle-Axe to break ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny nations in pieces.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider, and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 With thee also will I break in pieces man and woman, and with thee will I break in pieces old and young, and with thee will I break in pieces the young man, and the maid.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 I will also break in pieces with thee the shepherd, and his flock, and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman, and his yoke of oxen, and with thee will I break in pieces cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains and rulers <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The sense of all these three verses is the same, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That God had made use, and was still making use of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> to waste and to destroy many nations, to spoil and impoverish much people, wasting their goods, routing their Armies, kil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling all sorts of their inhabitants.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And I will render unto Babylon, and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea, all their evil that they have done in Zion, in your sight, faith the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The particle in the front of this verse which our Transla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tors (understanding the four former verses of <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi>) render <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> in a copulative sense, must be rendred <ns0:hi>now</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>but,</ns0:hi> i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the four former verses be understood of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and the sense is this. Though I have hitherto made use of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and shall yet for a time make use of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy several other nations, yet now the time is come<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that I will punish them, and recompence to them all the mischeif they have done to the Jews and some of the Jews shall live to see it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:64" />25 Behold, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> against thee, O destroying mountain, saith the LORD, which destroyest all the earth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is not here called a Mountain because it was scitu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ated upon any Hills or Mountains, for it appears from <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> 11.2. that it was scituated in a plain, and we read <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 13. that it dwelt upon many <ns0:hi>Waters,</ns0:hi> but because it was very <ns0:hi>high</ns0:hi> for its Power, and Greatness and had very high Walls and Towers, that it looked at a distance like an high rocky Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, and as some say (being a very large City) was full of Trees. They had destroyed many people of the Earth that lay near to them.</ns0:note>, and I will stretch out my hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">God threatens to destroy them notwith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing their Towers, and great Fortifications, as many times they threw down Malefactors from high Rocks, Mountains, and Precipices.</ns0:note>, and will make thee a burnt mountain <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And to make them like <ns0:hi>Aetna</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Vesuvius,</ns0:hi> or like some other Mountains of Sulphur, or other bituminous matter fired, which are alwayes burning or else he<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> threaten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth that their Cities and Towers which appeared like a Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain should be burnt.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations, but thou shalt be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>everlast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing desolations.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> desolate for ever saith the LORD <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">God threatneth to <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> an utter ruine, and desolation so as they should not have a stone left fit to lay a Foundation; or to make a corner stone: or as some others interpret it, that City should never be built again, there should never from the Rub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bish of it be taken a stone to lay the foundation, nor to lay up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the corners of new Houses, new Walls, new Towers in that place. Foundation Stones, and Corner Stones, are principal Stones in Buildings. Nothing shall be left in <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> of any worth, value, or considerableness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet amongst the nations <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">These former words of this verse are expounded by those that follow, setting up of standards and blowings of Trumpets, are preparatory to bring Armies together. The setting up of Standards, and blowing of Trumpets are Military signs of the Will of those <ns0:hi>Princes</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Captains</ns0:hi> General whose those Standards are, and to whom those Trumpets belong, that those Souldiers who are under their Command should ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther themselves together to the places where those Standards are set up, and those Trumpets blown.</ns0:note>, prepare the nations against her, call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">What this Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Ararat</ns0:hi> was,</ns0:note>, Minni, and Ashchenaz <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And those of <ns0:hi>Minni</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ashchenaz</ns0:hi> is very hard to determine, we read of a mountain called <ns0:hi>Ararat,</ns0:hi> where the Ark rested after the Flood, <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> 8.4. Of <ns0:hi>Minni</ns0:hi> we read no where else; most Writers think these were two Kingdoms within <ns0:hi>Armenia. Ashchenaz</ns0:hi> descended from <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Iaphet, Genesis</ns0:hi> 10.3. certain it is that the Emperour of the <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>des,</ns0:hi> had the Dominion of these places, from whence it is very probable that either <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Darius,</ns0:hi> or both drew out Souldi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers to help them to conquer the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, appoint a captain against her <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">After people are gathered together for War, the first thing to be done is to put them into Military Order, constituting a Captain Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral.</ns0:note>, cause the horses to come up as the rough caterpillars <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Let the Horses come up like the rough Caterpillar.</ns0:hi> Others read it like the wasting Caterpillar, or like the horrible afright<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Caterpillar. Great disputes there are amongst critical In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpreters what <ns0:hi>Caterpillars</ns0:hi> are here meant, the Caterpillars be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing generally smooth; but as we know not the complexion of Insects over all the World, so even amongst us we see some Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpillars that look a little rough, that which alone we are here to attend is why the <ns0:hi>Median Horses</ns0:hi> are compared to these In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sects, undoubtedly it is either with respect to their numbers, for Caterpillars in those Countries used to come in vast num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers. 2. Or in regard of the horror and trembling caused by them in people when they came, being a great Plague to the places which they infested.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Prepare against her the nations with the kings of the Medes, the captains thereof, and all the rulers thereof, and all the land of his do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minion <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Here the Prophet declares those particular Princes, and Nations that should be Gods instruments to destroy <ns0:hi>Babylon, viz. Cyrus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Dari<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s</ns0:hi> the Emperours of the <ns0:hi>Medes,</ns0:hi> with all the Forces under their Command, and people under their Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And the land shall tremble and sorrow <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That is, <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> or the Land of <ns0:hi>Chaldea</ns0:hi> shall tremble and sorrow.</ns0:note>; for every purpose of the LORD shall be perform<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon a desolation without an inhabitant <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">For God hath determined to destroy it, and to leave it wholly desolate, so as none should dwell in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 The mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight, they have remained in <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> holds, their might hath failed <ns0:note place="margin">Is<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 19.16. chap. 50.37.</ns0:note>, they became as women <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">When God hath determined an end, he ordereth means proportionable to that end. <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> had many v<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>iant and mighty men, and it is very probable the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry much to them, but when it came to, God took off their courage so as they had no heart to fight but kept <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hemselves in their strong holds, and, if at any time they came out, their courage failed them, and they behaved themselve<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> more like Women then Men of War, so as their Enemies burnt their Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties, brake down their Fortifications, and made what havock they pleased.</ns0:note>: they have burnt her dwelling places, her barrs are broken <ns0:hi>t.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the king of Babylon that his city is taken at <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> end <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">We have had occasion once and again to recite what we have in Civil Historians about the taking of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Cyrus, viz.</ns0:hi> That it was taken by surprize, by the <ns0:hi>Median</ns0:hi> Emperours unexpected diverting the River <ns0:hi>E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>phrates</ns0:hi> by divers Channels which he cut; as also that <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> was a very vast City, the greatness of which might admit of Post, and Messengers from one end of the City to another to acquaint the King what was done at the other end of the City in which himself was Resident, and it is said that the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> when his City was taken, did not know of his danger until the Enemy had entred the City.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And that the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 50.38.</ns0:note> passages are stopt <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">This was part of the message which the Prophet saith the Messenger should carry to the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> that was in the other part of the City, that the passages over the River <ns0:hi>Enphrates,</ns0:hi> or any other passages by which the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> might, upon the Enemies entrance, make their escape, were all stopped, and guarded with Souldiers, or otherwise so as there was no hope of any making an escape.</ns0:note>, and the reeds they have burnt with fire <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>Reeds</ns0:hi> signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies also standing Pools of Water, and that some judge the sense, the water is drained out of the pits or pools so as it could not hinder the entrance of the Enemies, those that adhere to the translation of it <ns0:hi>Reeds,</ns0:hi> say that upon the borders of the River <ns0:hi>Euphrates</ns0:hi> were vast quantities of great and tall Reeds, which with the mud in which they stood, were as another Wall to the City, but the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> had burnt up them so as the way was open to the Walls, and the Men of War,</ns0:note>, and the men of war are afrighted <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Seeing these reeds burnt up, and the water drained from them, were afrighted, so as their hearts through fear failed them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, The daughter of Babylon <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> like a threshing floor <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> had been a threshing instrument, by which, and a <ns0:hi>threshing floor</ns0:hi> in which God had threshed many other Nations, God now intended to make it as a threshing floor wherein he would thresh the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>in the time that he thresheth her.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> time to thresh her: yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Some think because of the next words that the words were better translated <ns0:hi>it is time to tread her,</ns0:hi> (so the word properly signifies) as men use to prepare their threshing floors against the time of Harvest, for the time of this Harvest was near, <ns0:hi>her Harvest</ns0:hi> signifieth the Harvest which the Justice of God would have from the ruine of the <ns0:hi>Chal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deans.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured me, he hath crushed me, he hath made me an empty vessel, he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />licates, he hath cast me out <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Prophet speaketh this in the name of the Jews com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plaining of the <ns0:hi>King of Babylon</ns0:hi> as the author of all the miseries they had indured, which he expresseth by several phrases signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fying the same thing, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That it was the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> that had ruined them, and filled himself and his Souldiers with their delicate things, and cast them out of their Land dealing with them as Wolves or other Beasts of prey, that eat what
they please of other Beasts they have preyed upon, and leave the rest in the Fields.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:65" />35 The <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>my vi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> violence done to me, and to <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the remain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> my flesh, <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> upon Babylon, shall the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>inhabi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ss.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> inhabitant of Zion say; and my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea, shall Ierusalem say <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The words are either a Prayer, or a prediction of Gods vengeance upon <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 137. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7, 8. God hath said vengeance is his and he will repay it. The Church of the Jews here commits its cause to God, and prayeth him to execute vengeance for her. How far it is lawful for us to pray against our Enemies, we have heard once and again.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 Therefore thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will plead thy cause, and take vengeance for thee <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Men had need take heed how they give cause of appeals to God against them, especially the appeals of such as are a peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple that have a Covenant relation to God. God in those cases ordinarily sheweth himself a <ns0:hi>swift witness</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iudge</ns0:hi>; and gives a speedy judgment in such causes. Behold saith God I will plead thy cause, not with words, but actually with my judicial dispensa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, therefore it is expounded by taking vengeance.</ns0:note>, and I will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 50.38.</ns0:note> dry up her sea, and make her springs dry <ns0:note place="bottom">The vengeance which God threatneth is expressed <ns0:hi>metaphorically</ns0:hi> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />der the notion of <ns0:hi>drying up her Sea,</ns0:hi> and making her <ns0:hi>Springs</ns0:hi> dry, which signifies the depriving her of all necessaries, not only of the abundance of her Men, Riches, Treasures, but of her Springs. Thus I had rather expound it, then as referring to the particular stratagem by which <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> took <ns0:hi>Babylon, viz.</ns0:hi> By drying up in some measure the River <ns0:hi>Euphrates,</ns0:hi> that is turning it into other Channels.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And Babylon shall become heaps <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Heapes of Rubbish.</ns0:note>, a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 13.22.</ns0:note> dwelling place for dragons, an astonishment and an hissing without an inhabitant <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 50.39, 40. where the s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>me thing wa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> before said.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 They shall roar together like lions: they shall <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>shake them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> yell as lions whelps <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">It is incertain whether this be to be understood of the <ns0:hi>Medes,</ns0:hi> making horrible roarings and noises when they took <ns0:hi>Babylon:</ns0:hi> Or, of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> who upon the taking of their City (as is usual) made horrid outcries as being a people quite undone, some think it referreth to the drunken noises of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> at their Festival, during the celebration of which we are told their City was taken, but to this one would think the comparison of <ns0:hi>Lions whelps</ns0:hi> (which ordinarily yell for want of victuals, or for some mischief done them, not when their bellies are full) should not so well agree.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 In their heat I will make their feasts <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">When they shall grow hot with Wine, I will put or give, or make them a Feast of another nature. Interpreters judge that the Prophet referreth to the Feast made by <ns0:hi>Belshazzar, Dan.</ns0:hi> 5.1. <ns0:hi>To a thousand of his Lords,</ns0:hi> when he and his Wives, and Concubines drank Wine in the vessels belonging to the Temple, during which Feast the City was taken.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">verse 57.</ns0:note> I will make them drunken, that they may rejoyce, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not awake, saith the LORD <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">So they were made drunk with the wine cup of Gods fury, because the Lord had designed them to utter ruine, and destruction, that as men filled with Wine are merry, and shout, and then fall asleep; so the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> being drunk with the Wine of the Lords wrath, while they were merry with their Cups of Wine might fall into such a sleep as they should never awake out of.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with he goats <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That is, they shall be destroyed before they are aware of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 How is Sheshach <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">We meet with this term <ns0:hi>Sheshach</ns0:hi> only here, and chapter 25.26. both places leave it doubtful whether it be to be taken for an Idol which they called by the name of <ns0:hi>Shach</ns0:hi>: or a name given to the City of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> which worshipped that Idol, to the honour of which the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> kept a yearly Festival for se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral dayes. In the time of which Festival they say it was that <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> took the City of <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> taken? and how is the praise of the whole earth surprized <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> that was so famous over all the World for her splendor.</ns0:note>? how is Babylon become an astonishment among the nations <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And so it is interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in the next words, wherein <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> for the punishment brought upon it is said to be an astonishment to all Nations, which makes it probable that <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is what was called <ns0:hi>Sheshach,</ns0:hi> by the doubling of a letter, because she worshipped <ns0:hi>Schach.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 The sea is come up upon Babylon: she is covered with the multitude of the wa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>es thereof <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">A multitude of Enemies, that are like the Sea in which there is a multitude of waters or that will over-run them as the Sea overfloweth the shore, or any land into which it once breaketh.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness, a land wherein no man dwelleth, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther doth <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> son of man pass thereby <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.6. and 9.12. the words are all of them de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scriptive of an utter desolation, that should not onely be the fate of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> the head City, but of all the inferiour Cities that were as daughters to that mother City.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 And I will punish Bel in Babylon <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Bel</ns0:hi> was the principal <ns0:hi>Babylonian Idol,</ns0:hi> of which see what is noted <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 50.2.</ns0:note>, and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">All the Vessels of the Temple 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 36.7. and what ever gifts the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> had presented to him.</ns0:note>, and the nations shall not flow together any more unto him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It was the custom of other Nations to send presents to the Gods of those Nations whom they were in subjection to, or whom they would appease; whence it is that we read the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> when they had the Ark would not send it home without a present, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6.11. God by his Prophet foretelleth that the time should come when the Nations should come no more to <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> either to pay an homage to their chief Idol, nor yet to bring offerings unto him.</ns0:note>, yea the wall of Babylon shall fall <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And the City of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> should be also ruined.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 5<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6. Rev. 18.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul from the fierce anger of the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These words are an exhortation to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> to be wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling upon the first proclamation of Liberty by <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> to go out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> notwithstanding the pleasantness of the place, and that now their stakes had been pitched there many years, because of the ruine which should most certainly come on that place.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 And lest your hearts faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And lest they should be affrighted by the Succession of E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vils year after year that should come upon <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi> Some think it were better translated, <ns0:hi>And let not your hearts faint.</ns0:hi> Though you should hear of <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> his coming year after year, yet faint not (for they say <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> was one year preparing, and that he spent the second year in passing through <ns0:hi>Assyria,</ns0:hi> so as he came not at <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> till the third year) no not though you should see or hear of successive troubles, and a great deal of violence in the land by the opposition of great Princes one to another, for none of them shall do you any harm, but this doth not so well sute<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to the former verse, where they are bid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />den to make haste out, and to save their own lives, I do there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore prefer the sense of our interpreters and their Translation of it, as making another Argument to perswade them to make haste out, because they would by reason of the successive evils year after year coming upon the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> live there very trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blesome and uneasie lives.</ns0:note>: a rumour shall both come <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> year, and after that in <ns0:hi>another</ns0:hi> year <ns0:hi>shall come</ns0:hi> a rumour, and vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence in the land, ruler against ruler <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 Therefore behold, the days come, that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>I wil visit upon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> I will do judgment upon the graven images of Babylon, and her whole land shall be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />founded <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">I will do, that is, I will execute Judgment upon the Idols of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and the whole land of <ns0:hi>Chaldea</ns0:hi> shall be confounded, when they shall see that their Idols will do them no more service.</ns0:note>, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Some in stead of <ns0:hi>her slain,</ns0:hi> would have it read <ns0:hi>her dancers</ns0:hi> (for the City was taken while <ns0:hi>Belshazzar</ns0:hi> and his whole court were Revelling) but the learned Author of the <ns0:hi>English</ns0:hi> Annotations tells us the word will not bear it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 Then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 44.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. and 49.13. Rev. 18.20.</ns0:note> the heaven, and the earth, and all that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> therein shall sing for Babylon <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">All the Creatures in Heaven and Earth shall rejoice at the Vengeance which God shall take upon <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> which had been the destroyer of so many of their People.</ns0:note>, for the spoilers shall come unto her from the north, saith the LORD <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Median</ns0:hi> Souldiers are those here called spoilers from the <ns0:hi>North.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:65" />49 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>both Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>to fall, O ye slain or Israel, and with Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> As Babylon <ns0:hi>hath caused</ns0:hi> the slain o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> Israel to fall, so at Babylon shall fall the slain of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e c<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ntry.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> all the earth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The words in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> have some difficulty which is not so obvious to those not acquainted with that Language, but hath given occasion to Interpreters to vary in their particular Translations of it, but they mostly agree in the general sense. <ns0:hi>viz</ns0:hi> that these words are given as a reason why the whole earth should so much rejoyce in the ruine of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> because <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> had caused <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> to fall, the latter term <ns0:hi>all the earth</ns0:hi> must be understood in a restrained sense, for <ns0:hi>that earth</ns0:hi>; the <ns0:hi>Caldeans</ns0:hi> coming up from all parts of <ns0:hi>Chaldea</ns0:hi> to help <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi> should be slain there, as by the means of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were slain that came up from all parts of <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> to help <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 Ye that have escaped the sword, go a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way, stand not still <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">It is hard to resolve whether the Prophet here speaks to the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> though most understand it of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> whom God would have leave <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> as soon as they should have a liberty proclaimed.</ns0:note>: remember the LORD afar off <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">And to remember when they came in to <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> the great things both of Justice toward the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> and Mercy toward them, which God had done.</ns0:note>, and let Jerusalem come into your mind <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And keep <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> in their mind, as the place where they were to worship God according to his direction, and for which God had so wrought.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 We are confounded, because we have heard reproach <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The words of this verse seem to prove that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were the Persons intended in the former verse whom God would have to go away, and not to stand still, for it is out of doubt, that it is of them the Prophet here speaketh, and whom the Prophet brings in here, saying, <ns0:hi>we are confounded,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>ashamed</ns0:hi> (as it is expounded in the next words) to hear the Enemies reproaching us, for our God, or for our Religion, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 137.3. And</ns0:note>, shame hath covered our faces: for strangers are come into the sanctuaries of the LORDs house <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>because</ns0:hi> Pagans that were strangers to the Commonwealth of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who <ns0:hi>Numbers</ns0:hi> 1.51. might not come near the Tabernacle of the Lord, were come, and that not to <ns0:hi>worship,</ns0:hi> but to plunder and rifle in the <ns0:hi>Sanctuaries of the Lord,</ns0:hi> even into the Court of the Priests and of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and into the most Holy Place, those whose very presence in these places had been a pollution of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">52 Wherefore behold, the dayes come, saith the LORD, that I will do judgment upon her graven images, and through all her land, the wounded shall groan <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For which complaints of my people, or rather for which profanation of my Holy Place, I will be revenged upon their Graven Images, and not onely upon their Idols, but upon the Worshippers of them, and cause a groaning of wounded men over all the country of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> I will cause them to know that their Idols are not able to protect them from my Power and Justice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="53">53 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Obad. 4.</ns0:note> Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortifie the height of her strength, <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> from me shall spoilers come unto her, saith the LORD <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">We are very prone to measure things by the measures of our own Reasons, and to judge of events which are to be the effects of Divine Power, by humane probabilities, therefore God is put to use many words to the same purpose; he saw the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> saying in their hearts, How can these things be? <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> hath impregnable Walls<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> two hundred foot high (so Historians report) and of a great breadth, and it hath very strong, and high Towers; God by his Prophet tells them, that if they could mount up as high as Heaven, if they could make their Towers much stronger than they were, yet the <ns0:hi>Spoilers</ns0:hi> were to come from him, and he could and would send spoilers, who would pull down her Walls, and break down her Towers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="54">54 A sound of a cry <ns0:hi>cometh</ns0:hi> from Babylon, and great destruction from the land of the Chal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deans <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To assure them that what God threatned should certainly be, he calls to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> to listen as if already there were a cry from <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and a sound of a great destruction from the land of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="55">55 Because the LORD hath spoiled Babylon <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The sword is not so much the s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ord of the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> as the sword of the Lord. It is he who is to be looked at, as the spoiler of <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and destroyed out of her the great voice <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And hath made to cease in that great City the noises caused from multitudes of people in it walking up and down, and traffiquing together.</ns0:note>, when her waves do roar, like great waters, a noise of their voice is uttered <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The noise of her E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nemies that shall break in upon her shall be like the noise and roarings of the Sea, when it dasheth upon the shore or upon some Rocks. That shall be the onely noise shall be heard in her, instead of the Noises wont there to be made from the multitude of people, or from Revellers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="56">56 Because the spoiler is come upon her, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken <ns0:hi>t,</ns0:hi> for the LORD God of recompenses, shall surely requite <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Little more is said here than was before, onely the words hint the taking of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> by a surprize when the King, and the Inhabitants were not aware of it, which we had before al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so told us, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 39, 40.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">In this the Prophet saith, that God would act but as a just God, a <ns0:hi>God of recompens<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s,</ns0:hi> where Gods people suffer wrong, and either cannot revenge them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, or may not do it, being private Persons (to whom God hath given no power of the sword) if they can exercise Faith and Patience, they shall find God a God of <ns0:hi>Recompenses,</ns0:hi> that can and will requite their Enemies, and plead their cause.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="57">57 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 39.</ns0:note> I will make drunk her princes, and her wise <ns0:hi>men,</ns0:hi> her captains and her rulers, and her mighty men, and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the king, whose name <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the LORD of hosts <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Drunken men use to fall asleep. The Prophet speaks here metaphorically. His meaning is, that the Lord would fill them with the <ns0:hi>wine</ns0:hi> of his <ns0:hi>fury</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>chapter</ns0:hi> 25.15, 16. and upon the drinking of it they should sleep their last sleep, the effects of it should be their utter ruine and destruction. Yet there seemeth to be an allusion to the posture the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and the Thousand of his Lords mentioned, <ns0:hi>Daniel.</ns0:hi> 5.1. was in, when their City was taken (which as was before said) was in the time of the Festival of their Idol <ns0:hi>Shach</ns0:hi>) when they were drinking wine in the Bowles that were brought from the Temple at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem, verse</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 30. it is said, <ns0:hi>In that very night was Belshazzar the King of the Chaldeans slain.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="58">58 Thus saith the LORD of hosts, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the walls of broad Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>made na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ked.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken, and her high gates shall be burnt with fire <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Incredible things are told us by Historians of this great City. They say the compass of it was threescore Miles about. That her Walls were in height two hundred foot, in breadth such as two Chariots might drive a breast upon the top of them, that it had an hundred great Gates, many of them of Brass, God threatens the breaking down of these Walls, and the burning of these high Gates and Towers.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hab. 2.13.</ns0:note> the people shall labour in vain, and the folk in the fire, and they shall be weary <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">And that though the People should labour to quench this fire, or to rebuild this City, yet it should be all lost labour, and they should give over their enterprise, as being weary.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="59">59 ¶ The word which Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah, the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of this <ns0:hi>Seraiah</ns0:hi> we read no more than we have in this verse<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> though <ns0:hi>Chapter</ns0:hi> 36.26. there be mention made of a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother <ns0:hi>Seraiah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, when he went <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>on the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />half of.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> with Zedekiah the king of Judah into Babylon <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">We no where read of any journey <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> made into <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> till he was carried a Prisoner thither, it is therefore probable that <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> should be translated <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> as the same particle is in other places, <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> 4.1. and 44.4. it being not usual with great Princes to make visits one to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther at such distances, though the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> tell us a story of some such thing.</ns0:note>, in the fourth year of his reign <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The expressing of this Circumstance of time, lets us know that this Prophesie was many years before <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon</ns0:hi> was destroyed, for it was seven years before <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was taken; so as it must be above sixty years before it was fulfilled in the first degree.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> Seraiah <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Prince of Menucha</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>chief chamber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lain.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> quiet prince <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word admits of various Interpretations, some think that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> was a place over which <ns0:hi>Seraiah</ns0:hi> had some Authority under <ns0:hi>Zedekiah,</ns0:hi> the same with <ns0:hi>Manahah,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chronicles</ns0:hi> 8.6. Others think it was a name of Office, and signified <ns0:hi>Lord Chamberlain,</ns0:hi> but the best Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters see no reason to vary from our Translation, the sense of which is that he was a man of a moderate quiet temper, that perswaded to peace.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="60">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:66" />60 So Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come upon Babylon, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> all these words <ns0:hi>that are</ns0:hi> written against Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bylon.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="61">61 And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, When thou comest to Babylon, and shalt see, and shalt read all these words <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not to the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> nor possibly is it to be understood of a meer private reading of them to himself, but to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> that were in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> acquainting them with what God had spoken against <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> by the Prophet.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="62">62 Then shalt thou say, O LORD, thou hast spoken against this place to cut it off, that none shall remain in it, neither man nor beast, but that it shall be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>desola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> desolate for ever <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Thou shalt testifie that thou believedst what thou hast read to be what shall most certainly come to pass, by speaking words to this Sense.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="63">63 And it shall be when thou hast made an end of reading this book, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou shalt bind <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Rev. 18.21.</ns0:note> a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Eu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phrates.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="64">64 And thou shalt say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">It hath been often said that <ns0:hi>Euphrates</ns0:hi> was that great River which ran by the Walls of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi>; into this <ns0:hi>Seraiah</ns0:hi> is com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded by <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> to throw this Roll of Prophesie against <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> symbolically to teach the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> that according to the Tenor of his Prophesie the time should come after some years, when <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> should be destroyed never to rise again to any great view, or degree of splendor, no more than that Roll with the Stone tied to it should rise from the bottom of <ns0:hi>Eu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phrates.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: and they shall be weary <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Some read though they weary themselves, that is do what they can, or (as it is here) and they shall be weary with that weight of Judgment which shall be upon them:</ns0:note>. Thus far <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the words of Jeremiah <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either the words of <ns0:hi>Ieremy</ns0:hi> relating to <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> reach thus far, or all the words of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> remaining on Sacred Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cord (for it is thought that the next Chapter was rather penned by some other Holy Man.) Or (which seemeth the best) the Prophetical words of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> for the matter of the next Chapter is Historical, and the book of <ns0:hi>Lamentations</ns0:hi> is not Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phetical; as to the main of it, though there be in it three or four Prophetical passages, <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 4.21, 22, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
            </ns0:div>
